speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that I have received the following letter from the secretary of His Royal Highness the Governor General:
Office of the Governor General's Secretary, Ottawa, February, 16th, 1912.
Sir,-I have the honour to inform you that the Eight Hon. the Chief Justice of Canada, acting as Deputy to His Royal Highness the Governor General, will proceed to the Senate Chamber this afternoon at 3.30 o'clock for the purpose of giving the Royal Assent to

certain Bills which have passed the Senate and the House of Commons during the present session of parliament.
I have the honour to he,
Your obedient servant,
H. C. LOWTHER, Lieut.-Colonel,
Governor General's Secretary. The Honourable, the Speaker
of the House of Commons.
Mr. WHITE (Leeds) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

Before you leave the Chair, I would like to draw the attention of the House for a few moments to the question of cable rates. This question has already come before the House in a previous debate, but I thought this occasion favourable for bringing it again to the attention of the country. We all know that the news received some months ago, through the channel of the Post Office Department, that cheaper nates had been granted toy the cable companies was welcome news to Canada. When it was announced to the House by the Postmaster General, I was the first one to congratulate him over this signal success of or# many efforts to obtain a reduction in the rates. For several years past, and notably, since the time of Sir William Mulock until the present, there has been a continuous effort on the part of our postal authorities to join hands with the many British subjects abroad who are interested in the solution of this problem, namely, cheap telegraphic communication between the mother country and the various British colonies. I said, however, to my hon. friend the Postmaster General when he announced some weeks ago that a small reduction in rates had been agreed to by the cable companies and the British government, that in my judgment it was but one instalment, and that we should expect more from future pourparlers between the companies the British Post office and our own post office authorities in Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would like to say to the hon. member (Mr. Lemreux), before he speaks further, that it seems to me doubtful whether lie is not infringing a well understood rule of the House by anticipating a discussion of a notice on the order paper. The hon. member or Lamb-ton (Mr. Armstrong) has a notice on the order paper which now stands at the head of Public Bills and Orders.
Further consideration of the proposed resolution of Mr. Armstrong (Lambton), that, in the opinion of this House a commission should be appointed to investigate the systems of national telegraphs and telephones, wireless telegraphs and cables.
A discussion took place on that resolution, and now stands to be resumed. I would like to be advised by the House whether it is the judgment of the House that the hon. gentleman is or is not infringing the rule which would prevent another discussion taking place at the present time.

I somewhat anticipated the objection, hut I thought that, as the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) had a fixed purpose io his motion, that of the appointment of a commission to investigate these various questions and problems, my own motion-because I will conclude with a motion-would be in order. Of course, the hon. member for Lambton has mentioned several questions in his motion, while I desire to draw attention only to one of those subjects.
I think our purposes are different. My hon. friend .moves for a commission; I wish simply to obtain an expression of the opinion of the House my motion treads as follows:
That in the opinion of this House steps should he taken by the Postmaster Genera] of Canada with a view of obtaining further reduction in cable rates between Canada and Great, Britain.
I do not think the two motions clash.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish again to submit the question to the judgment of the House. While there is considerable force in what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) says, I >am not fully convinced that his motion is not an infringement of the rule. But if it is the desire of the House that the hon. member should continue, of course the Speaker lias no objection.
I am in the judgment of the House. If my hon. friend the Postmaster General sees no objection I might be .allowed to proceed.

The motion standing in the name of the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) seems to be along the same line as the motion of the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), whose motion, it is true, refers to only one of the many branches contained in the motion of the hon. member for Lambton. Personally I have no objection to this mutter being gone into. If the hon. member for Rouville wants a discussion of the matter in the House, it might help us <pn the other side of the sea to know the opinion of the House of Commons of Canada, I suppose the hon. gentleman does not intend to press the motion very far. I do not think there could be much objection to his going on; anyway, I hope he will be short.

As there seems to be some differ-v ence between the new motions, as this

is an important subject, and as the time to be occupied will not be very great, perhaps it might be considered in order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. gentleman continue the debate?

Before that motion is passed I would say that I think it would only have been fair to the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), to have had notice that this discussion was to go on so that he could have taken part in it. I understand that, under the rules of the House, he is debarred from continuing the discussion which he was obliged to drop at six o'clock on a Wednesday night, and which he will not be permitted again to take up. But, if the hon. member for RouviMe (Mr. Lemieux), is to be permitted this afternoon to discuss the same question, I think it only fair that the hon. member for East Lambton should have notice. He should have been notified, and he should have been given an opportunity of being here to take part in the discussion and to continue his speech to the end.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think that is fair, perhaps under the circumstances, and as my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), does not appear to be here, it might be convenient to postpone it until another day. When I suggested that the discussion might go on I was not aware that my hon. friend was not here.

I do not wish to press the matter, but I may say that I understood the other evening that the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), was allowed to proceed with a motion of a similar nature which dealt with one of the many subjects mentioned in the omnibus motion of the hon. member for East Lambton, and it seems to me that the same rule should prevail.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not suggesting that it should not prevail, but I was suggesting that it would, perhaps, be convenient to postpone the debate until my hon'. friend from East Lambton is here.
Under the circumstances I bow to the desire of the Prime Minister. We might fix a day when this question might be brought up. I have no objection under the circumstances to the postponement.
Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Ottawa-grounds, $25,000.

['The appropriation is the annual one for the care of the parliament grounds. I stated the other day in the House that the government had not yet come to any conclusion as to the use to be made of that space on Sussex street acquired by the late government, nor has it come to any conclusion as to the plans for erecting a departmental building. A Committee of the Privy Council has been named to give the matter careful and prompt attention, but it has been utterly impossible during the progress of the session for that committee to give such a large subject the attention it requires. We will proceed in the matter as soon as possible. The late government acquired that site on Sussex street several years ago, and yet, so far as we have been able to discover, it had not formulated any plan for erecting buildings there. If the lion, gentleman wishes to know what I think myself, I may say that it has occurred to me that we might utilize that space which has been so long idle, and in which we have made such a large investment, for the erection of a justice building, which would accommodate the Department of Justice, the Supreme Court, the Railway Commission, the Exchequer Court, and all other branches jn connection with the administration of justice. There was a plan prepared by Mr. Maxwell, architect of Montreal, for -a very handsome Justice Department building on that space on Sussex street, and I think it might be properly erected there, leaving large open spaces around which would give a park effect. It is out of the question to hope that we could put all the departmental buildings that will be required on that long narrow strip of land, and it puzzles me to know how such a thing could ever have been contemplated. We are considering the acquisition of other lands where a departmental building might suitably be erected.']

This item of $25,000 is asked to be voted to make provision in ac-Mr. BORDEN.
cordance with an estimate submitted by the chief architect for keeping the grounds in connection with the public buildings, the Lover's Walk, Major Hill Park, and the mint and archives buildings, in proper condition during next year. For the grounds of Parliament Hill the estimate is $14,000, and for Major Hill Park $11,000.
Is there any plan of the work to be done in these grounds? I understood there would be a bridge connecting this side of the hill with Major Hill park?

There is a project of that kind, but that does not enter into the calculation of this estimate. I can give my hon. friend the details if he wishes them. This is the usual appropriation for plants, pay-lists, lawn mowers, arc lamps, electric lights and repairs.

I am glad that my hon. friend has mentioned arc lamps in Major Hffll park. At the present time Major Hill park is not .lighted. I am glad to see that my hon. friend has taken some measures towards lighting it. We had some pour parlers with the city of Ottawa in regard to the lighting of the park. It has never been lighted up to the present time. Nepean Point park is li g%d by the commission but the other park lias not been lighted up to this time and the park has been of very little use to the public, because it could not be used at night. Has anything been done with respect to the matter?

I had that question under consideration two or three days ago, and I asked my officers to look up the deed of agreement between ourselves and the city of Ottawa in regard to Major Hill park so as to make sure of the ..unclitions under which we held that park. I believe there is an old deed between the city of Ottawa and the government in regard to the park. At any rate, we have placed in the estimates an item of $139 for additional arc lights in that park.

As I understand the deed, I do not think the city of Ottawa will dispute that they are bound to light the park-I never understood them to dispute that point-but what they wanted was to have a plan showing where the lights should be placed. That was the condition of things when we left office and I am very glad to hear the hon. gentleman has taken the matter up because the hotel will be ready early in May and we will be deprived of a great deal of the advantage it will be to the city if the park is not. lighted.

What does the government intend to do with the grounds which

were expropriated on Sussex street to form the site of the new departmental buildings? There has been quite an agitation in favour of leaving this space vacant so as to round off the parliament grounds and make it a sort of a park. Does the minister intend to erect the departmental buildings on this vacant place or is he expropriating land elsewhere for that purpose?

The appropriation is the annual one for the care of the parliament grounds. I stated the other day in the House that the government had not yet come to any conclusion as to the use to be made of that space on Sussex street acquired by the late government, nor has it come to any conclusion as to the plans for erecting a departmental building. A Committee of the Privy Council has been named to give the matter careful and prompt attention, but it has been utterly impossible during the progress of the session for that committee to give such a large subject the attention it requires. We will proceed in the matter as soon as possible. The late government acquired that site on Sussex street several years ago, and yet, so far as we have been able to discover, it had not formulated any plan for erecting buildings there. If the hon. gentleman wishes to know what I think myself, I may say that it has occurred to me that we might utilize that space which has been so long idle, and in which we have made such a large investment, for the erection of a justice building, which would accommodate the Department of Justice, the Supreme Court, the Railway Commission, the Exchequer Court, and all other branches jn connection with the administration of justice. There was a plan prepared by Mr. Maxwell, architect of Montreal, for -a very handsome Justice Department building on that space on Sussex street, and I think it might be properly erected there, leaving large open spaces around which would give a park effect. It is out of the question to hope that we could put all the departmental buildings that will be required on that long narrow strip of land, and it puzzles me to know how such a thing could ever have been contemplated. We are considering the acquisition of other lands where a departmental building might suitably be erected.

A message was delivered by Major Ernest J. Chambers, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Right Honourable the Deputy of His Royal Highness the Governor General desires the immediate attendance of
your honourable House in the Chamber of
the honourable the Senate.
Accordingly, the House went up to the Senate Chamber.
And having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER informed the House that His Honour the Deputy of His Royal Highness the Governor General had been pleased to give in His Majesty's name the Royal assent to the following Bill:
An Act to amend the Manitoba Grain Act.
House in Committee of Supply.
['All right.']

When the present government assumed office, we found that we were paying a very large amount as rental for accommodation in the different parts of the city of Ottawa. The amount has increased greatly within the last five or six years, and more space is wanted. At present. I believe, there is not one department in Ottawa that is adequately accommodated, and every day requisitions are made to the department for further accommodation. The departments are broken up one part of a department being in one building and another in another, so that communication between the segregated branches of the department becomes inconvenient and costly. It seems to be absolutely necessary for us to settle now definitely what space we shall require for the erection of departmental buildings, and to begin that -erection without -delay, so as to avoid as far as possible incurring new liabilities for rental, although I do not imagine that it will be possible even if we -begin building next summer, to continue mucjh longer without leasing additional space for the accommodation of the departments. This work the government will undertake as soon as it has been relieved of its sessional duties.'
Mr. jLEMIEUX. The hon. gentleman has mentioned some eastern ground. Will he please state where it is located?
The ground around the three main buildings here.

Surely my hon. friend does not anticipate such vandalism. I am quite sure the public will be aroused if it learns that he intends to take any of that space for the erection of new buildings. We have gone, I think, to the very limit by the additions which have been made to the House oi Commons and to the Eastern Block. If my hon. friend has any feeling for the artistic and architectural beauty of the parliament buildings, he surely will not encroach further on the remaining land.

My hon. friend misunderstood me. There is no thought of adding

to the present buildings except some addition to the Library. The idea is to acquire land to the east of the present buildings on which to erect new buildings.
Would that be on Wellington street?
In that direction. I cannot speak positively, because nothing has been decided.

If the hon. gentleman contemplate erecting a building on Sussex street for the Supreme Court and the Department of Justice and the Railway Commission, might not the space at present occupied by the Supreme Court building be utilized for the proposed extension?
Undoubtedly.

I would like to call the minister's attention to the fact that the long-distance telephone at present in the basement is very inconveniently placed for the use of members. If there is any way by which the minister can have it placed on this floor, near the Chamber, it would be a matter of great convenience, I am sure, to every hon. member of the House. I would be much pleased if he would immediately direct some of his officers to look into the matter.

I will attend to this request. I .may say that as soon as we are free I intend taking up the question of the installation of telephones generally for government purposes. We pay from $20,000 to .$23,000 >ifor telephone service. It has been suggested to me by several who have some knowledge on these matters that our whole telephone system needs to be reorganized in the interest of both comfort and economy.
What does my hon. friend mean by saying ' when we are free?' Is he not free now?
My right hon. friend surely knows what I mean. It is extremely difficult during the sittings of the House to attend to the matters that have been referred to.

In view of the fact that there are so many telephone connections with the parliament buildings and the public offices generally, would it not be well for the hon. gentleman to have prepared a special telephone directory covering the several departments and the House of Commons?

I do not think that it is in that direction that we can very much improve, because the present telephone directory seems to be very correct. I have been told, however, that we might have one, two, or three exchanges-for instance, one in each block by which means com-Mr. MONK.
munication would be much easier and more prompt, and there would also be a great saving of public money.
I would like to ask if it is the intention of the government to build a customs house next summer at the town of Dauphin, in Manitoba?

I cannot answer that question off-hand. I do not think it is the intention of the government to proceed with that construction this year; but the supplementary estimates are not yet completed. If my hon. friend can give me a special reason for that construction, we will consider it.

I would like to take this matter up with my hon. friend at some time. It is very important that there should be a customs house built there in the near future, and it is not necessary to buy any land for the purpose, as the new building could be erected on the ground on which the post office is now built. At present the post office is in an upper room, and it is not very convenient.
Is the maintenance of the parliament grounds done by contract?
No, it is done by day work, I believe, as in the past.
How many men are employed for that work?
About 25.
When were the men appointed whose names figure on that list?

I have not on this list the date of appointment of each of the men, but I am under the impression that there aTe men who have been employed for quite a long time. Most of them are employed during the summer. I do not think there have been any appointments lately. I can give the names to my hon. friend, but I have not the date of appointment. _ There has been no appointments lately in this branch of the Public Works that I am aware of.

Does the minister take care that competent elevator men are selected? Are they required to undergo an examination as to their ability to run an elevator safely, or are they appointed merely on the recommendation of the members for the city?

They are _ not appointed merely on the recommendation of the members for Ottawa, and they are chosen only after they have undergone careful examination by the heads of the branch. As a rule these employees are very competent and capable men.
Who examines them?

We have a superintendent, and I think his name is Mr. Shearer. The elevator men, I may say, are fully tested. Although we may make mistakes sometimes, I have had no complaints at all about these employees except that one of them was past the age when a man could carefully handle an elevator. That case will be investigated.

Those of us who come from distant parts of the Dominion and are immured on the third floor have to use the elevators very frequently, and especially on Saturday." Referring more particularly to the elevator which is used by the public who go to the galleries, the man in charge, and who has been there since Christmas, is not only incompetent to discharge that duty, but he lacks the necessary intelligence which every elevator man should have. This elevator is probably used three times as much as any other elevator in the building, and I would suggest that this man be removed and stationed somewhere else. I think those in charge of elevators should be bright and intelligent young men, who, in addition to a knowledge as to how to run an elevator, should possess some additional features of intelligence that would render them useful servants. Another complaint I would make is that on Saturday, when the elevator is most required, the man goes away. I would ask the Minister to give instructions not only to place a proper man in charge of this elevator, but that it shall be kept running on occasions like Saturday when it is so much in demand by members from a distance.

I will make a note of the remarks of any hon. friend, and we will try and see that the difficulties of which he complains are remedied. Of course we cannot expect to have perfect men in charge of elevators.

The question is a more serious one than the hon. minister seems to think. Elevator men are usually subject to very severe examination because the lives of the passengers who use the elevators are in their keeping. In all large cities a rigid examination is required by the civic authorities. In the city of Montreal no man is appointed to take charge of an elevator without having passed a very severe test, I would call the minister's attention also to the fact that the elevator men smoke whilst on duty. This is objectionable to members of the House and also for the ladies who use these elevators. On one or two elevators which I have occasion to use daily the elevator, men may be seen smoking vigorously, and the smoke they puff is quite offensive. That is not at all respectful to members, and these men should be compelled to discontinue the
practice. I have also noticed other officials, probably recent appointees, indulging in smoking in the lobbies. You would not see that in any great building owned by a corporation or controlled by a legislature. You never see elevator men, watchmen, and any officials smoking and puffing their smoke as do these men in this building.
Now, as we are talking about elevators, might I mention that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) dismissed the elevator man in the eastern block soon after he .took office. The man is a good officer, works faithfully, from early morning till late in the evening. But he was seen speaking with some of the ex-Cabinet ministers, and, of course, was spotted at once by the spies, and his head was cut off by the guillotine erected by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) on Parliament hill. This man is the father of thirteen children-it seemed to be an unlucky number in his case. But, fortunately, this country has as Prime Minister, a man with a big heart, He'found the head in the basket, replaced it on the shoulders of the poor elevator man-for this purpose acting over the head of the lord high executioner -and reinstated to his old post, the father of thirteen children. In the name of the country, and especially on behalf of those who have large families, I thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) for his kindly act.

The minister has evidently had previous notice of the incompetency of one of the elevator men, and, apparently, the one to which the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) referred. There was no justification for the appointment of such a man to the place he holds, and I submit to the minister (Mr. Monk) that he had no right to take time to consider the matter of the man's dismissal. He ought never to have been appointed, and he ought to be dismissed.

My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean, Halifax) is not so generous, apparently, as the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). The only report I had about this man was that he is afflicted with old age. I am very cruel, perhaps, but I do not dismiss men because of their age alone. The matter was mentioned to me by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Boyer) who thought that this man was too old to be able to handle the crowds that use that elevator. I thought that deserved investigation. If my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean, Halifax) thinks the man is so thoroughly incompetent that he must be dismissed at once, I will take that into consideration; but I do not think that on the strength of a passing remark I should have dismissed him at once. But I will look into the matter. As regards the state of affairs reported here by my hon. friend about dismissals, I can only say that it is absolutely with-

cut foundation. Notices were sent out to some employees in the Public Works Department. Representations were made to me and I at once appointed an investigator, one who seemed to me a mir minded man, and to that investigator every man was entitled to go and explain his case, whether he had received notice or not. The man to whom my hon. friend referred came before this investigator, and it was found that there was no ground for removing him. There are a number of other similar cases. The investigation is going on, and nobody has been dismissed without investigation. Every man in my department has an opportunity of laying his case before the investigator. Some of them are assisted by counsel, as I believe my hon. friend is aware. That is very different from what happened at the last change of government.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) refer to Mr. Chauvin's investigation?
Yes.
He is the one who investigates these cases in Ottawa? Now, has my hon. friend a list of the day labourers who are appearing before Mr. Chauvin? In other words, has he the black list?

The list of those charged with infraction of the rules of the department was placed in the hands of the investigator, and the parties were invited to go to him and explain the accusations made against them by members of parliament and others.
Are parties permitted to be represented by counsel?
Certainly.

The man appointed by the Department of Railways and Canals in the eastern part of Nova Scotia to conduct these dismissals is a partisan so violent that I have no hesitation in saying, on the responsibility of my position, that he is not the man to hear or adjudicate on any matter involving questions of party politics. He will not permit counsel, nor^ will he permit the party to ask a question of the witness, unless that question is first submitted to him; and if he does not approve of it, he will not put it. I am glad to know that in the Public Works Department methods different from those of the notorious Judge Jeffreys are followed in these investigations. I take this opportunity of calling the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) to the fact that the Jeffreys methods ought not to be encouraged or permitted in the Railway Department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not had my attention directed to any such matter. I shall inquire into it. I am afraid the commissioner referred to by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald, Pictou) must have been misled by the example of the late Insurance Commission.
He should not follow a wrong precedent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. But I did not hear my hon. friend's voice raised against the action of that commission. I am glad that we discern in him the symptoms of a newly-awakened conscience.

I do not wish to get into a general discussion. But I think that when I made such a statement as I have just made, the Prime Minister of this country should not rely upon so old-fashioned a method of reply as the tu quoque argument. I think he has pretty thoroughly exhausted that form of reply. It must surely seem clear to him that the course taken by the Public Works Department, of which we have the assurance of the minister (Mr. Monk), is the one to be followed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it is; and I have said that I will inquire into the matter the hon. gentleman mentions. At the same time, it is proper to call attention to the fact that, under a commission of very wide-reaching powers issued by the late administration, precisely these methods were adopted.
Not into an inquiry into partisanship.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is a distinction without a difference. However, apart from that, I agree that every person who is under investigation should have an opportunity of being represented by counsel and of cross-examining witnesses if he desires to.
Would the right hon. gentleman say, if a case is not proven, who should pay the costs? The poor day labourer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is a question upon which I would not like to pronounce an opinion at the moment; I do not know whether there is any precedent in regard to that. It is, however, a fair matter for consideration.

I would like to ask the Prime Minister what disposition he will make in cases where a man is declared to be innocent. Will he restore him to his position again? I have had some cases in the Marine and Fisheries Department, in my constituency, where lighthouse keepers have been turned out of office

without trial. In one case the minister has agreed to give a trial; he informs me that the man has protested that he is not guilty of any partisanship, and he will give him a trial. There is not much use of our going through the expense of a trial unless it amounts to something afterwards.
I would like to have the Prime Minister's view of a case in which nothing whatever has been proven against the official, and he has been dismissed after trial.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No case of that kind has been brought to my attention. If any such case shall arise, it will be a matter, in the first place, for the head of the department. Eventually it might have to be considered by the government.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Last week I was present at two investigations being held by the Commissioner of the Railway Department. In both those instances Mr. Lane told the gentlemen that they con'd be represented by counsel if they wished.

I am quite prepared to believe that. I know Mr. Lane, who is an old schoolfellow of mine, and 1 would expect him to do that. The gentleman whom I referred to is Mr. Duchemin, and I did not expect him to do it, from what I knew before; and I am not surprised to learn that when he did undertake to do it, the commissioner said he didn't do it. Therefore, I call the attention of the Prime Minister to the case.

I would not like to lay down the principle that an investigation is to be granted in all cases, far from it.
I was induced to do that here in Ottawa because there was so great a number of complaints. It was alleged that the employees of my department had been turned into a regular political organization, of which I have the proof. I stated on previous occasions that it is extremely unfair and cruel for candidates to insist that public employees, poor day-labourers, men who would not meddle in politics, men who drive a team or who are engaged in a similar humble occupation, should necessarily attend committee meetings, go out canvassing, and represent the candidate at the polls. These things are all forbidden, and I say that any candidate who asks a public employee to do that is committing a great injustice, because he knows what the consequences are. But where the minister is perfectly satisfied that these practices have been resorted to, and that an employee has infringed the rule, violated the regulations and laws, is the government to investigate simplv because the employee asks it to investigate, although the minister is perfectly satisfied without an investigation? That would involve the country in immense expense, 103	REVISED
without any utility whatever. Something must be left to the discretion of the head of the department. I had a case where a good employee was accused, and I thought I had convincing proof that he had been an active partisan and had violated the regulations. I explained the law to him, he was a good man with a family; he insisted that there was no proof whatever against him. I caused an investigation to be made-it must have cost $300 or $400, I suppose, when all the expenses have been paid, and there was evidence absolutely uncontradicted, that he had violated the regulations. That case is still pending before me. I do not admit, therefore, that in every case there must be an investigation. In Ottawa there were a very large number of men accused, and when I saw the number and knew that the accusations might or might not be well founded, as I could not investigate them myself, I named an investigator. I am satisfied that justice will be done.

All these expressions of sympathy from the hon. minister are very good, but what we are concerned with now is to secure a fair investigation in all cases so that justice may be done. As far as the commissioners are concerned, I am afraid there is too much in what my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has said. I am afraid that in some cases the partisanship of the commissioner gets the better of his judgment, and causes him to conduct investigations in a manner that would not be tolerated in any judicial inquiry. I could instance a case with which the commissioner to whom the hon. member for Pictou has referred had to do. He did not confine himself to the charges that were made against the person to be investigated, but he constituted his court a fishing commission. He goes around looking for evidence against others than those against whom charges are made; he tries to ascertain who constituted the executive committees and controlled the party organization in certain places. He inquires who are the men that had contributed towards legitimate election expenses and furnished teams, &c. He is an inquisitor, and goes outside the functions of a court. I saw a copy of the evidence in a certain case that was taken before the commissioner referred to by the member for Pictou, and I have described the nature of the investigation he was conducting in that ease. He was supposed to investigate a charge of offensive partisan-shin against a man whose position somebody else wanted, and he went on with an inquiry into the conduct of the whole campaign in that locality. I think that, in addition to giving the accused an opportunity of being heard in his own defence. it is only right that these commis-EDITION

sioners should confine their inquiry to the specific charges made. Surely any person who makes a charge of partisanship and tries to take the means of a man's livelihood away from him, though the latter is only exercising his Tight of citizenship, should be prepared to make his charge specific, and not go outside it.

There is one matter I have for some time wished to bring to the notice of the Prime Minister, namely, his understanding of what is meant by an ' official '. It always occurred to me that a man who works with pick and shovel around these buildings, shovelling snow, or doing some menial work of that kind, can hardly be called an official. I notice that, in a discussion which took place on the 6th of December, the Prime Minister gave two reasons for his decision on this point. He gave two grounds, one was a section of the Civil Service Act of 1908; the other a resolution of this parliament. The section of the Civil Service Act which he read was:
No official, clerk or employee of the Civil Service shall be debarred from voting at any Dominion or provincial election if under the laws governing the said election he has a right to vote. But no such officer, clerk or employee shall engage in partisan work in connection with said election.
The resolution which the right hon. gentleman read was this:
That while it is desirable that every official in the employ of the government of Canada should enjoy perfect freedom of political opinion and the untrammelled exercise of his franchise in accord therewith, no official should be engaged or be permitted to engage in partisan work of any description in the election of a representative to the provincial or the Dominion legislature.
In the first place, he deals with those who come within the operation of the Civil Service Act, and who are not allowed to take any part in election campaigns, or otherwise interfere politically. The provisions of the Civil Service Act do not take in such men as I have mentioned-men working on the sections of the Intercolonial railway, doing ordinary day-work, and men who are handling freight in the freight sheds of the Intercolonial railway, or loading cars. Men of that kind are not covered by the provisions of the Civil Service Act, and they would not be subject to dismissal under that section. In the same way, the resolution dealing with officials certainly does not contemplate men who are working round the grounds here, shovelling snow, or running elevators.
Does the hon. gentleman want us to understand that men doing this particular kind of work should be at liberty to take part in elections?

I think that every man who is earning $1.50 or $2 a day has a perfect right to do what he pleases, and that be should not be interfered with because he is politically one way or the other. I certainly say that it is degrading and bringing too low the idea of government supervision in this country to interfere with men in matters of this kind.
What about the interest of the public?

I do not know that when a man cuts a drain so many inches wide and so many feet long and does a good day's work, or when a man shovels so much snow'and does it well, the public is particularly concerned as to what his mental outfit is politically. I do not think that it would interfere with the character of the snow shoveling or the water carrying capacity of the drain. The hon. member for Lincoln might have a different idea.
I learned my idea in Lincoln where the late government dismissed everybody without cause.
I am not aware that the late government has ever dismissed a man from employment of that kind.
Oh, oh.
In Lincoln county they dismissed everybody.

I am not familiar with what has taken place elsewhere, but in the part of the country from which I come such a thing certainly has not happened. We have the Intercolonial railway from the Strait of Canso to Sydney, and I defy the hon. gentleman to name one man who was wonting at day's labour on that road who was dismissed by reason of his poliltics. The records of that stretch of road, which is the only part of the Intercolonial railway of which I can speak with knowledge, are before him, and he is at liberty to inquire into them. I am not, at all events, addressing any person in particular except the Minister of Public Works and the Prime Minister, and I say that the line of demarcation should be drawn somewhere. There should be some distinction between a head officer in a department who is getting a big salary and has a comfortable position, and the man who is doing small things. If he does his work well I think it beneath the head of any department to interfere in a case of that kind.

I understood the other day from the Minister of Public Works, that under no circumstances-he was very emphatic-had a man been dismissed without being given an investigation, if he claimed the privilege. That statement was published broadcast in the press and im-

Let me ask the hon. gentleman if this wandering Scotchman ever stopped to contemplate the fact that he was paid by the government to work at something else than being deputy returning officer that day, and that if he had been performing the service for which he was paid he could not have acted as deputy returning officer in the election, I suppose, in the interest of the people who appointed him.

My hon. friend is a very good lawyer; at least I was told so the other day by the Prime Minister that he was so good a lawyer that his cases are submitted to the Privy Council. I will have this case submitted to the Privy Council.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman surely knows that there are certain rules enacted for the governance of the House and its committee, and the Tule which is invoked by the Chairman is a very plain one. Had my hon. friomd from Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) been presenting something which was not in connection with the Department of Public Works it would be out of order, but we are now discussing the public works estimates, and anything which refers to that department is quite in order. The question is whether the minister who is now at the head of the department has or has not done something which ought to be discussed in parliament. Marine and Fisheries, but certainly when these dismissals have occurred in the Department of Public Works the discussion is in order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think that is a very fair statement of it, but the right hon. geu-tleman surely knows that we have been wandering over every department of the government.

The matter to which I am about to refer comes under the Public Works Department. The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) when discussing the dismissal of a public servant who was of that nationality, has spoken about the Scotch people being clannish. But I am now going to bring to the attention of the House the case of a French Acadian. I may say that in the province of Nova Scotia we have a large number of French Acadians, and better citizens in every respect we have not in this country, it is remarkable that the only French Acadian in the employ of the government on the dredges was dismissed by the present government without an hour's notice. He was dismissed within a very few days after the present government took office; he was harshly treated, he was given no notice that there was any accusation against him, and he was not allowed an opportunity to defend himself. When the Minister of Public Works tells the House that he did not dismiss any employee without charges being made and without an inquiry, the minister is labouring under a misapprehension. It is my opinion, after reading the papers, that in tins ease the minister was imposed upon and deceived. But, that is a very good reason why the minister should proceed very carefully in these matters, and not take the word of some person who may have a grudge against an official, without making due inquiries. In this case, the captain of the dredge ' Cape Breton ' was dismissed without any explanation, or without any charge having been made against him, and so when he seeks employment elsewhere naturally the first question asked him is, where was he last employed, and if it is ascertained that he was dismissed without the reason therefor being assigned, then he might be suspected of incompetency, or dishonesty. It was in order to vindicate this man to some extent that I moved for the papers, for of course I had no expectation that he would be reinstated or that justice would be done him by this government. I believe that the result of making the facts public will demonstrate that there is no stain on the reputation of Captain Decoste. Let us see the evidence on which this man was dismissed. There is

here a letter from Thomas Gallant, who was Conservative candidate in Inverness last election, and the letter was written on October 14, very shortly after the present government came to power. In that letter Mr. Gallant says:
I would beg leave to recommend that Captain Peter Decoste of the dredge ' Cape Breton ' be dismissed and Captain Dan Gillis of Port Hawkesbury succeed him. Captain Gillis is a most capable officer. He was dismissed in 1896 for absolutely no reason but that he favoured the Conservative party.

Hear, hear.
Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish)'. Hon. gentlemen say:	' hear, hear ' but I will
have something to say about that later on. The letter continues:
I think I can safely say that all the members from the Island of Cape Breton and eastern Nova Scotia are thoroughly in accord with this proposition.
Yours very truly,

Now, if it were true that Captain Gillis was dismissed in 1896 for no other reason than that he favoured the Conservative party, it would be a very high handed act on the part of the Liberals and possibly Captain Gillis should be reinstated. But the record of Captain Gillis must have been in the department and there is nothing here to show that the Minister of Public Works examined that record to find out whether the reason given for the dismissal of Captain Gillis in 1896 was the right reason. As a fact, the record will show that that was not the reason why Captain Gillis was dismissed, and, as to the statement in the letter that all the members of the Island of Cape Breton and eastern Nova Scotia are in favour of Captain Decoste's dismissal, it is only necessary to point out that all these members are Liberals, and it is not likely they would ask for the dismissal of one of their own friends and the reinstatement of a man who was said to have been dismissed solely because he was a Conservative.
Would not these Liberal members ask for the dismissal of their own political friend if it was in the public interest?

Your mind is too acute for me, I cannot follow you. I can say it is not true that a single one of the members from the Island of Cape Breton or the eastern part of Nova Scotia asked for the dismissal of Captain Decoste. I may say in justice to Mr. Gallant that probably what he really meant was that the defeated Conservative candidates at the last election and not the members from the Island of Cape Breton and eastern Nova Scotia wanted to have this gentleman dismissed, and the other statement was probably an error in typewriting. I do not think that Mr. Gallant intended! to misstate the facts because 1 know him to be a thoroughly respectable gentleman and one who would not deliberately mislead the Minister of Public Works or any one else. But I think he was used as a tool in this case., that he was imposed upon, that he was not seized of the actual facts before writing the letter. And there are other letters on the record which sustains this assumption or belief on my part. There is a letter from one William Macdonald, president of the Pic-tou Conservative Club, who says:
As far as I know, the whole of eastern Nova Scotia and Cape Breton insists on this appointment.
That is, the appointment of Captain Gillis. It is evident that there is some fine Italian hand behind the attempt to get Captain Peter DeCoste out of his position. How is William Macdonald in a position to speak for the whole of eastern Nova Scotia and Cape Breton? But to show how confident these men were of being able to secure anything and everything they wanted from this government in the way of beheading unfortunate Grits, he winds up his letter by saying:
Kindly communicate your decision to me as soon as possible, as Captain Gillis is at present here.
They could not wait for an investigation; there was no suggestion that an inquiry should be made. All that these men wanted was the place for Captain Gillis, and they felt sure that the minister would fall into the snare and do what was asked without an inquiry. Next I find a letter from J. A. Gillis, who was the Conservative candidate in Richmond county. I mention this tof remove any idea that Thos. Gallant tried to deceive the department. Mr. Gillis says:
I beg leave to recommend the dismissal of Captain Peter Decoste of the dredge ' Cape Breton ' and the appointment in his place of Captain Daniel Gillis of Port Hawkesbury, Cape Breton, at present of Piotou, Nova Scotia, Captain Gillis is an exceptionally competent man and was dismissed without cause in 18-9S to make way for Decoste.
What is the first tiling that the minister should have done when he received that letter? Should he not have inquired whether it was really the case that Captain Gillis had been dismissed without cause in 1896? T cannot find any evidence to justify that statement. You will also observe that there is not a single scintilla of evidence to show that Captain Decoste wjas a partisan, or was in any way offensive to the community.
Air. DAVIDSON-Why was Captain Gillis dismissed?
The records of the department are there, and the minister will be prepared to explain that, I presume.
You said that the statement made by Mr. Gallant that- this man *was dismissed without cause was incorrect.

I made the statement that the minister should have 'looked up the records and ascertained whether that statement was correct or not. He had no right to assume such an alleged fact. I will go further to satisfy my hon. friend, and will say that Captain Gillis was not dismissed because of offensive partisanship. He was continued by the late Minister of Public Works as an employee on one of the government dredges up to the day of the election; after the day of the election, and up to the time he took the place of Captain Peter Decoste. I would be sorry to say anything against Captain Gillis. I think he is a pretty good Liberal, 'but I hope that will not hurt him, and that the minister will not dismiss him from the service on that account.	He was dismissed for other reasons.	I think the
member for Cumberland county made some charges against him, but they were not charges of offensive political partisanship. I do not want to go into that, because I do not want to say anything against Captain Gillis. But I do blame the Minister of Public Works for not having ascertained whether the charge made in these letters which I have read, was correct or not, that Captain Gillis had been dismissed for political partisanship; and I blame him for dismissing Captain Decoste without any accusation having been made against him. He should at least have insisted that J. A. Gillis, Thomas Gallant and William Macdonald and the others disclosed and undisclosed or some of them should have made a charge that Peter Decoste was guilty of offensive partisanship and on that account was not entitled to remain in charge of the dredge 'Cape Breton.' All through this correspondence you will not find one hint or suggestion that Captain Decoste was an offensive partisan, or that he had done any wrong, according to the standard by which the minister has been judging officials since he came into office. I-find a letter here from John McCormick, who also was a defeated Conservative candidate in North-Cape Breton, as follows: I
I beg to recommend the dismissal of Captain Decoste of the dredge ' Cape Breton ' and the appointment in his place of Captain Daniel Gillis of Port Hawkesbury Cape Breton, who 'in 1896 was dismissed without, cause to make way for said Decoste.

How does he know that Captain Gillis was dismissed without cause? There is no doubt that he was sincere in the matter, but why did the minister act on this statement? Why did he not verify the facts for himself? You will observe that in this letter there is no hint or suggestion that Captain Decoste is a partisan. There is a similar letter from J. W. Maddin, the late representative for Cape Breton South, who goes one better. He says:
_ Captain Gillis is a man of great experience in the dredging business, and was dismissed in 1896 to make room for Decoste.
If that is so, it would be only right that Captain Gillis should be reinstated. Is it so, however? Where is the evidence of it from tlie record or otherwise? But if we go a little further, we find Finlay Macdonald, president of the county of Cape Breton Liberal-Conservative Association saying:
Captain Gillis is a most competent man against whom I believe no complaint ivas ever made. Captain Decoste's record you will he able to get from your officials.
Is this correct? Was there no complaint ever made against Captain Gillis? Here is another reason why the minister should have asked these men to make their charge against Captain Decoste, unless there was something in his record which satisfied him that Captain Decoste should have been dismissed. But I have a copy of all the correspondence relating to this dismissal, and I cannot find a single word against his record. Then, we have a letter from the Liberal-Conservative Association of Inverness county. In that letter it is said that Captain Decoste is a man of no experience whatever.' That is ridiculous. He has had experience under the late administration from the time he took the place until he was dismissed. His record was good, excellent,. But behind that he had the experience of a quarter of a century as a navigator and had the highest certificates. How was this dismissal brought about? The only information he had of it was in a telegram dated October 26, 1911, from the assistant engineer to Mr. Graham, the superintendent of dredging as follows:
Kindly arrange to have Captain Gillis of Port Hawkesbury replace Captain Decoste of dredge 'Cape Breton ' giving him all necessary instructions regarding his work.
Then Mr. Graham writes to the assistant engineer under date of October 27, 1911:
I am to-day in receipt of the following message from Mr. A. K. Dufresne, assistant chief engineer, Department of Public Works, Ottawa:-' Kindly arrange to have Captain Daniel Gillis of Port Hawkesbury replace Captain Decoste of dredge Cape Breton, giv-

mg him all necessary instructions regarding liis work/ The above telegram is self explanatory and I have instructed Captain Gillis to report at my office to-morrow morning in connection with the same. When Captain Gillis arrives at the dredge I will feel obliged of you will give him any information you can in connection with the work being performed at St. Ann's, and also as to the operation and maintenance of the dredge. On his arrival on board the dredge, Captain Gillis will take charge of the plant.
Evidently Mr. Graham felt that Captain Gillis was not competent to take charge of the dredge ' Cape Breton ' without first having received instructions from Captain Decoste-without first being schooled in the work to be done. Now, you will observe that immediately after this government came into power, or a very few days afterwards, the minister, without any investigation whatever, and without any notice to Captain Decoste, sends a telegram to Mr. Graham, the superintend. ent of dredging, and asks for the dismissal of this man, Captain Decoste. Tire mails in drae course would: be too slow; the lightning rapidity of the wires- had to be used. That 'Certainly wias high-handed dealing and gross injustice towards Captain Decoste. But I desire to say, in all justice and fairness to the minister, that I believe he was imposed upon. Possibly he read the letters, or somebody else read them for him, and then he assumed that there was a charge of partisanship against Captain Decoste.
He thought that these men who had written these letters would not ask for a dismissal on any flimsy charges, or without having some justification for such action, and he took it for granted, perhaps, that Captain Decoste was an offensive partisan, or that these letters contained an accusation of offensive partisanship. But the correspondence does not show any charge whatever against Captain Decoste. The whole thing is simply this: it was desired to make a place for Captain Gillis, and, therefore, Captain Decoste was removed. I would ask the minister whether in, justice to Captain Decoste, and in justice to himself, he will not insist upon charges being made against Captain Decoste first, that then tihe charges diould be communicated by the government to the accused, and that he be given an opportunity of exonerating himself.

I would ask the minister to inquire into the charges upon which Captain Gillis was dismissed. I am informed that he was dismissed not for political partisanship, but because of insubordination, or trouble of that kind, and I think the records will bear that out.

I must take the liberty of telling my hon. friend from Antigonish (Mr,
Chisholm) that in my opinion he is making a great to do about nothing. I can assure him there will be no investigation in the case of Captain Decoste; we are well rid of him. He was quite unfit for the work of commander of that dredge, and in any event he would not have been retained in command any longer. The proofs of Captain Decoste's unfitness are in the department.
If there are charges against him, why have those charges not been brought down?
There were complaints against Captain Decoste.
We have no record of it.

There is a record in the department where my hon. friend can see them. There are quite a number of reports and my superintendent of dredging told me that Captain Decoste was not a satisfactory man. I have no doubt whatever that he was an unsuitable man to command that dredge, and I would not have maintained him there anyway. As to Captain Gillis we will see. I have never pretended that there would be an investigation in all cases where charges were made against officials. What I stated the other day, and what I repeat to-day, is that in Ottawa no dismissal would be effective without the man accused having an opportunity of going before the investigator. Some notices of dismissal had been sent out, but the general order regarding inquiries was given, and Mr. Cliauvin was appointed to investigate every case without exception. I do not by any means intend to apply that rule everywhere. Where there is ample proof before the minister that the employee has transgressed, he will be dismissed without any unnecessary investigation. In Ottawa the circumstances were different. The charges covered over 100 cases, and I thought it was better to have a general investigation. And I was right in saying that in Ottawa no employee has been dismissed without an investigation of the charges against him; and in every ease where the investigator reports to me-some reports have already been presented but I have not yet had time to look into them-that the charge is unfounded, justice will be done, whatever notice the accused man may have received. Replying to my hon. friend from Cape Breton I would say that every man employed in my department has had clear intimation, whether he is temporarily or permanently employed, that he is not to become an offensive partisan. Violations of this notice will be treated in the same way without any exception whatever. Of course the hardship is much greater where the

person concerned is a permanent employee, but to make a distinction which my hon. friend invites me to make would be extremely unwise. The law is there, and the regulation is in force, that no man employed and paid by the public can meddle in politics whether his employment be of a permanent character or not, and I intend to adhere to that rule in my department as strictly as possible.
Is Mr. Chauvin paid a per diem allowance of $15 or is he paid so much per case?
All the investigators are paid the same per diem rate of $15.
How many commissioners are engaged in investigating charges against officials? Can the minister give their names?
I have not the names of all of them. If my hon. friend will move for that information it will be supplied to him.

I want to call the minister's attention, but not in any critical spirit at all, to the desirability of a public building for the town of Swift Current, and I trust that he will take the claims of that (dace into his consideration when he comes to prepare his supplementary estimates.

All the facts in regard to Swift Current were placed before me yesterday by a delegation, and they are now being considered by the officers of the department who have charge of the preparation of the suDplementary estimates.
Mr. KNOW'LES. I thank the minister for giving me that information, but I still deem it urgent and necessary to press upon him as strongly as I can the necessity for the construction of this building. The town of Swift Current has grown faster, proportionately, than any other town in Saskatchewan. It is a very important centre for the reason that no other town of any consequence is located within anything like reasonable distance of it. It is 111 miles from Moosejaw, and 89 or 90 miles from Maple Creek, and the territory to which it ministers extends southward for probably 100 miles, and northward for 50 miles. The town is going to be an important railway centre. The main line of the Canadian Pacific railway passes through the place, and construction of two other lines, one to run in a southeasterly, and the other, in a northwesterly direction, has been commenced. The amount of business that is transacted in the federal offices in Swift Current indicates the importance of the town.
