So the minister will see that there was a total revenue of well over $300,000 at Swift Current in the last year. I submit that the minister might well use that town very generously. If he will contemplate the enor-

mous revenue which is received by the government through this town, he must see that that puts the town in a different class from ordinary towns In the different parts of Canada. There are the two facts -a revenue of over $300,000 and nothing whatever in the shape of a public building. There is great need of a public building. The post office service suffers for lack of it and is very poor there at the present time. The Postmaster General is paying a large rent for accommodation there, also the Cugr toms and Interior Departments. It would be economical to put up a public building; it would be just to put up a public building, especially in view of the enormous revenue which comes to the treasury of this government from that centre.
Would the town give us a site?

I have not heard that point discussed. As a representative of the people I must say that 1 do not see why the town should be asked to give a site. The people of that town are paying up to the hilt in the way of customs and one thing and another, the town and district as I have shown, paying over $300,000. I should think that this is one of the towns in whose case the government would not be justified in insisting upon a site.
Many towns give us a site.

But very few of them can present so good a case as that which I have been able to make to-day. I doubt if he can show any other town yielding a revenue of over $300,000 and without anything in the way of a public building. The site need not cost a great deal. At the same time, I doubt if the town will give it. I have not consulted my constituents; but I would not recommend them to furnish a site when the town affords so large a revenue. I hope the minister will decide to buy a site; he could probably get it for $40,000. And I hope he will not think the cost of the site too much. A large sum besides this could be put into a public building and still keep within lines of economy. He could probably put up a building for $125,000 that would meet the present requirements of the town and reasonably anticipate the growth which is sure to take place there. I would ask the hon. minister to give me the assurance this afternoon that he wilt give the matter consideration with a view to providing means for a public building, not next session but this session, because the need is imperative and very urgent.
I think this is only another i'iustration of the maladministra tion or lack of proper administration during the regime of the Liberal party.
How so?

Here, according to the hon. gentleman is a most urgent case He pointed out the large revenue derived from Swift Current. But while these large revenues have been coming into the treasury for years and years past the government of which he was a strong supporter paid no attention to his request and left the town without proper accommodation for its business. I am surprised that the [DOT]hon. gentleman should make such am exhibition of the incompetence and neglect of the administration of which he was an ardent supporter. Had the place been represented by an opponent of the government, I should not have expected, under the rules laid down by the previous government it would pay much attention to his request. But there would be a candidate who would be responsible for bringing the claims of that town to the attention of the govereraemit. But this is only another illustration of the lack of interest of the late government in many parts of the country.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) is entirely in the dark. His assertion that this revenue has^ been received ' for years1 and years ' is without foundation. The Customs Office in Swift Current the Dominion Lands Office, and the Inland Revenue Office there are not two years old. If the hon. gentleman would come west he would understand that the conditions that prevail in my riding, have not existed ' for years and years ' to use his own beautiful expression. But the fact is that, had our Conservative friends in the last parliament not adopted that remarkably stupid 'System which they did adopt of obstructing all His Majesty's estimates, iit is probable the late government would have provided for the case. Prior to that, there was no great urgency and immediate need such as now exists. Perhaps the hon. member will take my word for it that he does not understand the condition. I presume that he knows something about Ontario that he thinks highly of it, and is highly thought of in that province. But he is absolutely at sea when he attempts to discuss the situation in a west-<>rn town. And I am sorry that he, so prominent a supporter of the government, should, in this indirect way, thiow cold water on my request for favourable consideration of this matter on the part of the government.
I am surprised, indeed, at what tlie lion, gentleman (Mr. Knowles) says, that the town of Swift Current is only two years old.
I did not say that.
Well, that the town was of no importance until two years ago- that is what I infer from what he says.
The hon. gentleman infers too much.
Then, I do not know what he did say. I remember going through that country twenty years ago, and I am pretty sure there was a place called Swift Current then.
The Tories were in power then; why did not they put up a public building?

It had not a revenue of $300,000 at that time. But it was growing and has grown very rapidly. The * current ' has been ' swift ' for the last two years, yet the government of which the hon. gentleman was such a swift supporter did not do anything to help the town to accelerate its motion. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles) says that we who were of the opposition of the day were responsible because we obstructed the estimates. Well, I do not know that the late government's majority ever came so low that any obstruction that we could offer would prevent them from putting an item through if they desired it. We criticised the estimates-very true. But I have no recollection of an item respecting Swift Current being criticised. The hon. gentleman has not told us that he had an item in the estimates for Swift Current. The probability is there -was no such item. So, the hon. gentleman has no right to find fault with the government for not giving attention to this important place. It is only an illustration, as I 'have said, of how the former government, when they thought they had a constituency absolutely certain to return a supporter, failed to give it attention. I am not opposing this estimate. The Minister of Public Works tells us that a deputation waited on him no later than yesterday and had presented the needs and demands of Swift Current more forcibly, if possible, than the hon. gentleman has presented them.
It was not necessary for the hon. gentleman to come forward at this time and repeat what- had been so well stated by the deputation, because the minister has all the facts, and probably the minister will listen to the deputation, and the hon. gentleman will find to his surprise that there will be a public building there-I will not say of the dimensions he speaks of. But is was a matter of curiosity to me why the hon. gentleman rose at all, when he knew that the government had .been already provided with the information, and that everything was going along smoothly. Perhaps he wanted to make a little cheap political capital by causing the people out there to think that the very forcible speech which he delivered this afternoon in support of a public building in Swift Current was the reason for its erection. I
hope the hon. gentleman will succeed in getting His building, proportionate to the size of the important town to which he refers.
We all well remember that when the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), was in opposition, he had a hardy annual request to the government then in power for something for his riding.
And I never got it.

My hon. friend is not finding fault with me because 1 haven't got it, but because I asked for it. Great as is my respec-t for that hon. gentleman, when I think well to ask for a public building I will ask for it, and I will keep on asking, and he can make Lis little speech as often as lie likes. It is a matter of absolute indifference to me. But my hon. friend knows nothing about the circumstances. Let me tell him that the town of Swift Current, although it did not give me a majority in 1908, in 1911 it gave me a majority of 80. I do not think the people will find that I am neglecting their interests. No matter what deputations may come down bare, I have my duty to discharge to my constituents.
I did not understand the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) to throw any cold water on this -request.
Not at all.

But he was -endeavouring to point out the real reason why the town of Swift Current was put off so long in getting this request. I have in my department a number of public buildings that are either being terminated or will have to be paid for, whose erection had been decided upon by the late government, but where one-tenth of the necessity did not exist that exists in the town of Swift Current, and where there is not one-third of the business done that is done in Swift Current, There is no doubt that the late government started upon a lavish erection of public buildings, and we have fallen into that hereditas damnosa, where there is nothing like the need that there is in Swift Current. It is surprising that the late government should go into those towns in the west where the price of sites is so terrifically expensive, where you have to pay for comparatively new towns, all the way from $40,000 to $125,000 for sites. It is astonishing to find that there was so little foresight in the last administration, and that they did not acquire sites at a time when they could have been purchased comparatively cheap. But they thought nothing of the future.

It is always difficult to predict what- changes will take place in a

country like Canada, and especially in the west. It is also hard to implement promises that have been made in the past. For instance, my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, who was so lavish in his promises when he sat on this side of the House of what he would do in the future, now that he is in office is very reluctant to implement those promises. The other day I asked what he was going to do with the harbour of Montreal, if he was going to make it a national and free port. My hon. friend said: No, not now, I am too busy, we have had no time to consider it.
I do not recollect saying anything of that kind.
Well, my hon. friend has no recollection at all, he is sleeping all the time. He promised his electors the Georgian Bay canal, to make Montreal a free port
That is coming quickly.
My hon. friend is like Rin Van Winkle. After sleeping for a century, probably he will wake up and find that all these things have been done, not by his friends, but by us.
Much you did for Montreal.

I would ask the Minister of Public Works what he proposes to do to give increased accommodation to the post office in the town of Yarmouth. The late government purchased a property directly south of the public building there, but I see nothing in the estimates this year for the extension of the post office so as to give the needed increased accommodation. I may say to the minister that the people of Yarmouth have complained for some time of the inadequacy of the post office quarters there. The late government purchased a building directly south, and it would require quite a sum of money to extend the post office to that building. I trust the minister, in his supplementary estimates, will put an amount sufficient to give this increased accommodation to the town of Yarmouth.
I will do my best.

I wish to bring another matter to the attention of the Minister of Public Works before this item is carried. Last November, I asked him why the captain of the dredge ' Cape Breton ' had been dismissed. He did not intimate that his services were not satisfactory, that he was incompetent, or that he had discharged his duties in a way that did not meet with the approval of the officers of the department. On the contrary he suggested that I should move for the papers in the matter. I got the papers, and read them to the House, and there is not a word in them to indicate that a
charge had ever been made during the whole fifteen years or thereabouts that Captain Deeoste was in the employ of the government. He never had any accident to his men during all the time that he was employed, he never lost a tug, or steamer, or any of the equipment used on a dredge. His record, to my own knowledge, has been good. If since the change of government, my hon friend the minister has discovered anything against the ability or the fitness of Captain Deeoste to hold that position, why didn't he bring those papers down with the rest of the correspondence?
I asked for all the papers, letters and correspondence in connection with his dismissal. I have a right to assume that all the charges that could be made against Captain Deeoste are found in the papers that are brought down, but there is not a single line in the form of a charge against him. Now it is decidedly unfair to Captain Deeoste that the minister should shift his position, and say: that might is right,
1 am Minister of Public Works, I am a member of a government with a strong majority behind me, and Deeoste must get along the best he can, he is only an insignificant French Acadian down in the county of Antigonish, and he lias got to face the music. Now, the minister practically says to those who inquire on behalf of Captain Deeoste that he dismissed him without having any charges made against him, and he refuses an investigation. I submit that such conduct is not what you would expect from a minister of the Crown, it is not compatible with those protestations of fairness and justice from the lips of the Minister of Public Works again and again since this session began. I submit that it is only fair to Captain Deeoste, that he should know what the charges are against him, and that he should be given an opportunity to vindicate himself.

My hon. friend is very lengthy in his complaint, but I do not say there were charges against Captain De-coste. I said that my officers reported to me that lie was a very unsatisfactory captain of the dredge. I can demonstrate that to my hon. friend if he will come to my office. I can show him the complaints

Are they in writing?
Mr. MONK

and produce before him
the officials of the department who will confirm what I am saying now. As to Captain Deeoste being a French Acadian, as alleged by my hon. friend, I may say that side of the question was never considered by me. He is probably an Acadian of French descent, and as such is extremely interesting to .me. But, there was no national question, fortunately, in this matter at all. I believe that Mr. Gallant is also an Acadian

by descent. Mt. Girouard is an Acadian. I believe, and ihe was dismissed in 189t without any reason whatever by my hon. friend and had to go and earn his live' lihood in the United States. I do not think that the national question will help my hon. friend very much in this matter.

I have the honour to represent several thousand French Aea-dians in my constituency adjoining the constituency of my hon. friend (Mr. Chisholm, Antigonish); I aim acquainted with Captain Decoste and I feei I should enter my protest againist what the minister has been saying with regard to him this afternoon. I was isorry to hear the minister say that Captain Decoste would not have any investigation. I do not say that because he is a French Acadian, but because he is a British subject and a good citizen of this country, a man who has the respect of his neighbours and of people generally in eastern Nova Scotia who know him. 1 think that for these reasons he ought to be accorded an investigation. The minister 'has told us that there are some charges against him by some officers of the department, which he has not produced to the House. It is a serious matter to Captain Decoste, it means his livelihood, it means his future, it means an end to his business ais a captain if the statement made >by the minister should go abroad and be believed by people who wished to employ Captain Decoste in the only capacity in which he is capable of serving. It is a very serious matter to him, and I do not think the minister was justified in stating so positively .that there would be no investigation into the case of Captain Decoste. The reason was that he had some papers, some statements in his possession

He was found an unsatisfactory officer.
Mr. SINCLAIR

reflecting on the character, I suppose, of Captain Decoste. If there are documents of that kind in the department I would remind the minister that the House passed an order that all documents relating to t'he dismissal of Captain Decoste should be produced. We have the documents here that were produced and we do not. find any complaint of that character. I do not think that this is a. position that the minister should take. I think he should say that he will bring down these documents and that he will give Captain Decoste ran opportunity of being heard.' It is not a question of getting back his job, but it is a question of his character, and that is very important to him. If he has an, opportunity of clearing up his reputation a.s a captain he might get employment somewhere else, but when the minister summarily discharges him Mr. MONK.
and states in parliament that here will be no investigation in Captain Decoste's case, it wall be a serious matter for Captain Decoste personally. I have a very high respect for him. He acted as captain of a dredge on work in my constituency, he gave thoroughly good service and there was no complaint against him by anybody. He did his work very well and I think there must be some mistake somewhere, because I do not think that Captain Decoste got fair play or that documents could be produced in the Public Works Department or anywhere else that would show that he was unfit to perform his duties.
I would like the minister to reconsider the decision that. he has come to this afternoon and to tell the House before this matter closes Drat he will give Captain De- -coste an opportunity of being heard for the purpose of clearing his character.
I did not say there were charges or accusations against this man. I said that he was an unsatisfactory officer by general report and that we did not consider that he was a loss to the department.

There is another matter that I want to mention to the Minister of Public Works and particularly while the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) is in his seat. Some years ago a person in the town of Digby was appointed by the Department of Public Works to attend to the winding of the clock in the public building in the town for which he was to receive $25 a year. I understand that he is in no sense a partisan and not considered as such in the town of Digby. Recently isonae person, whether by authority or not I do not know, placed on the door entering to the clock in the tower a padlock wfaidh prevents the proper person gaining access to the place where the clock is in order to wind it. This may he a very serious matter to the town of Digby if some day they ascertain that the clock in the public building is stopped. I would like the Minister of Public Works to look into this and instruct the man who put the padlock on the door to take it off so that the person employed some few years ago to wind the clock may have an opportunity of getting at it.
I will look into it.

I think that I will possibly be able to explain the situation to my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean). This gentleman to whom he refers as having charge of the clock in the public building at Digby has been reported to me as having been unsatisfactory. It was said that he did not care for the clock sufficiently well to keep it going, that at times it was, owing to lack of attention, stopped, and that otherwise it was not attended to

in a satisfactory way. I brought the matter to the attention of the Department of Public Works and the department removed that gentleman from office and appointed [DOT]another. The man who was appointed to -office received a notification to that effect, but through some oversight, as I am given to understand, the person who had previously held the appointment, did not receive notification. The result was that when the new official went to discharge his duties, after attending to them, he put a padlock on the door. The padlock, however, was removed by the gentleman who had previously attended to the clock. I think the matter has been explained to the satisfaction of all concerned by a notification from the department which has reached the first official to the effect that his services are no longer required.
He has been dismissed?
He has been dismissed.
And notified to that effect?
And notified to that effect.

I was not able to be present when the item of $100,000 for dredging and improvements in Yarmouth harbour came up. I would like to ask the minister what he proposes to do with the $100,000 that was voted, whether it is to be expended upon dredging or other work.
That is under consideration. The matter has not yet been decided, 'but I think dredging probably.

It seems to me that before the estimate passes the House we should be entitled to know something about the work that is to be done. There is an obstruction in Yarmouth harbour at Sollow's Rock ledge which has been there for many years and for the removal of which $75,000 was placed in last year's estimates.
Owing to the dissolution of parliament that money was not expended, and I would like the minister to state definitely now what he purposes doing with that vote and whether there will be an additional vote in the supplementary estimates. The port of Yarmouth is one of the most important in the maritime provinces; there are more first-class passengers landed there in the course of a year than at any other port in the maritime provinces or probably in the Dominion. We have a line of steamers now between Yarmouth and Boston and we are looking forward to having another line from Yarmouth to New York. The Canadian Pacific railway have purchased the Dominion Atlantic railway, including their steamship line, and it is proposed in a short
time to put larger boats on the route between Yarmouth and Boston, while of course the New York boats will also be larger than those plying at present to that port. I point out to the minister the urgency of the need of improvements at the port of Yarmouth. While the late government had been lavish in its expenditure there, and had greatly improved the harbour, yet there is a great handicap to shipping in the inadequate channel leading from the mouth of the harbour to the business part of the port. There is a ledge situated outside of the harbour on which there is at low water fourteen feet six inches, and that will require to be blasted out at a large expenditure. I submit to the minister that the necessity and importance of the port demand early action on the part of the government. There is considerable dredging also required in the harbour. We have in the channel a depth of twenty feet, but if the Canadian Pacific railway should put on larger boats as they intend to, a great deal of dredging will have to be done. The people of Yarmouth will appreciate the $100,000 which is now in the estimates, and I have nothing to say against it except that it is altogether too small. I trust that the minister, when he looks into the matter, will be able to place in the supplementary estimates an equal amount. When some gentlemen from Yarmouth attended the liquid banquet which was held in Halifax last fall, they said when they returned home, that they had seen the Minister of Public Works and the report was current that he intended to expend two or three million dollars on Yarmouth harbour, and although we appreciate the $100,000 in the estimates, the drop from two or three millions is great indeed. Has the minister any idea as to how he will expend the $100,000 in the main estimates?

I have a general idea, and that general idea which is very firmly imbedded in my mind is that when the late government spent- so much money in that locality it is a pity it did not remove that ledge to which the hon. member has referred. That was the key of the situation in the harbour of Yarmouth, and instead of employing the dredges in the neighbourhood _ of private docks, probably with the ob.ieet of advancing private interests, if they had removed the ledge at the entrance of the harbour it would have been a far more profitable service to the port. The port of Yarmouth will require our attention and there is a vote in the estimates for it.	,
The determination of the Canadian Pacific railw'ay, having acquired the Dominion

Atlantic line, to place new boats on the route, is not yet an accomplished fact. Although Yarmouth is an important port it is not the only port in Nova Scotia. There are other important ports along the Bay of Fundy, and until we know exactly what the plans of the Canadian Pacific railway are, and how far our improvements may meet these plans, the matter remains to a certain extent in doubt. Justice will be done to the harbour and certainly the work will be more profitable to the general interests of the port than anything done in the past by the late government.

In denial of what the minister has said, I wish to state that if he goes to Yarmouth he will only find a very few partisans who will say that the dredging done in Yarmouth Harbour has been dene for the benefit of private owners of wharfs. There has been no work done in the port of Yarmouth solely for the benefit of owners of wharfs; the work done there has been done in the interests of the general navigation of the port. I deny most emphatically the statement made by the minister. He has apparently been posted by some gentlemen from Yarmouth who have taken considerable interest in the matter, but I know that the statement he made to-day is absolutely wrong, I know that ninety per cent of the dredging done in Yarmouth Harbour has been done largely in the main channel, and while it certainly has improved private wharf property it undoubtedly has improved the harbour facilities as well. There was a channel dredged at the south end of the town which has opened up a largo fishing industry and I doubt if the Minister of Public Works will find even a Conservative in Yarmouth who will object to that work.
I know what I am speaking about and I say that the work done by the late government was done for the benefit of Yarmouth Harbour and was not done for the benefit of any private wharf owner. If the minister will spend this $100,000 to as good purpose as the late government spent the money, there will be no fault found. As to why the late government did not remove this ledge, I may say that there was only a certain amount of money voted and the dredging was done first, leaving it for the present government to take out the rock. Had the Liberal government remained in power, and I am sorry it did not-
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear hear.

Hon. gentlemen opposite may laugh, but if the rest of Canada had given as intelligent a vote as the County of Yarmouth did, we would have been on the other side of the House to-day. I feel [DOT]satisfied that had the late government been in power to-day I would have got a vote
of no less than $250,000 for the development of Yarmouth Harbour and if the present government puts that amount in the estimates they will be doing a lot of good in the public interest.

As a representative of one of the western Nova Scotia counties I wish to corroborate in a measure what has been said by my hon. friend from Yarmouth (Mr. Law). It is in the memory of this House that on a certain occasion when there ^ was to he a banquet in the constituency of my hon. friend (Mr. Law) and when the officers of the great Canadian Navy wore required there to furnish partners in the dance for the charming ladies of that locality, the ' Niobe ' was ordered to that port.
-Did notwithstanding the large expenditures of the late government for dredging in that harbour, it was in such a condition that the ' Niobe ' met with a very great misfortune.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. She met with no misfortune in the port of Yarmouth. What the hon. gentleman is stating is absolutely false, and he knows it.
1 would ask the hon. gentleman to take back that statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The statement should be withdrawn.
I say then that it is not in accordance with the fact.

The point I wish to make is this, that owing to the order given by my hon. friend, who wanted to make a day of it in Yarmouth, the warship ' Niobe ' .was despatched to that port. In carrying out that order she got into trouble and got the Dominion government into a great deal of trouble. Therefore I would like to see such expenditures made in that locality that not only would the people engaged in the dredging business be benefited, as I know they were by the expenditures previously made, but such improvements would be made in the port of Yarmouth and its vicinity that on the occasion of another visit to the port of Yarmouth, the Canadian navy, if it happened to be in existence at the time, would safely ride in and safely come out.

I do not want to allow the statement to go unchallenged that the ' Niobe,' before she left Yarmouth, met with a bad accident. The hon. gentleman will not hear that statement made in Yarmouth harbour or Yarmouth county. It has been made by the hon. member and circulated by every Tory newspaper in the Dominion of Canada, but I say that the ' Niobe ' met with no accident in the port of Yarmouth.

Mr. FOSTER (Kings, N.S.) Will the hon. member for Annapolis tell us what business the Niobe ' had at Yarmouth at that [DOT]time?
She was loaded with potatoes', apparently.

Before this item passes I would like to impress upon the hon. minister the necessity of doing some dredging at the Magdalen islands. Last year 1 obtained from my colleague the late Minister of Public Works the promise that a dredge belonging to the department *would be sent to the islands, and one was sent. As my hon. friend knows, there are several harbours around these islands, but the sands are continually shifting, so that the harbours are very difficult of ingress and egress. No dredge had been sent to the Magdalen islands since 1875, and it has always been difficult to obtain from the department the services of a dredge for that district, because the dredges were all monopolized by the various harbours in the maritime provinces. But, last year the late Minister of Public Works sent a dredge to the islands. The great difficulty, I am bound to say, is to get the work started at a stated point. Every man on the islands-I do not except my own friends - wanted the dredge to start in bis locality. This is a great mistake. There are certain harbours which should be attended to first, because the steamer stops at them.
What is the name of the dredge that is there?

I do not know the name. The resident engineer should select the places where the dredge should work. I told him not to be dictated to by any of the residents, but to follow' his owrn judgment. I may say that I lost heavily on the Magdalen islands because I followed the straight path and adhered to it from beginning to end. The dredge is still there, and I expect will be working next summer. The man who should be consulted in this matter is Captain McClure, the captain of the steamer which plies between Pictou and the various ports of the Magdalen islands. He lias prepared a map of the islands, which shows the places where the work should be done. I believe there is a duplicate of that map in the Public Works Department, and I would urge my hon. friend to give instructions to the resident engineer to follow the advice of Captain McClure, who is more experienced in such matters than any one else in that region.

Strong representations similar to those I have just heard have been made to me by the sitting member for the county (Mr. Gauthier), and we will endeavour during the coming summer to carry on the dredging in the wisest w'ay.

The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), says that about the bars and harbours of the Magdalen islands there are shifting sands. If that is the ease, no benefit will be obtained by dredging in the ordinary way. All that can be done is by dragging or harrowing. If the minister will consult the officers of the department, I think he would . find that they will agree with that statement.

It was a dredge used by the department for ordinary dredging, but in view of the shifting sands of the Magdalen Islands the then Minister of Public Works (iMr. Pugsley), sent a special dredge for the work.

When the estimates of the Minister of Public Works were under consideration before, I asked the minister some questions, and, if I remember correctly, he promised to furnish me with answers by letter. I have not yet received any communication from the minister, but I hope he will keep the matter in mind, and let me have the desired inlormation at his earliest convenience.

I got my officers to prepare answers to all the questions put during the discussion in committee that I was not able to answer at the time. I will put this information upon tire table so that hon. gentlemen interested can have access to it.
Ottawa-Heating, including salaries of engineers firemen and watchmen, $150,000.
What explanation has my hon. friend to give about this?

It is the usual vote, but somewhat increased this year. It is a vote to make provision for a large number of items of expenditure which are incurred every year in connection with the heating of the public buildings here.
What system of heating is adopted by the Public Works Department?
I believe there are hot water furnaces in most of the departmental buildings, and in others the heating is by steam.
How many firemen are employed?
We have 57 firemen whose wages range from $330 to $660 a year.
Has the minister dismissed a fireman named Gariepy?
I do not remember the name. If any complaint had been made against him, his name would be handed to the Ottawa investigator.
Why have the services of Mr. Williams, door-keeper at the door of this chamber, been dispensed with. This man is a British navy veteran, and possessed a number of medals gained in active service?

I know nothing of the circumstances and doubt very much if this man was in my department. If so, and there was complaint against him, his case would have been referred to the investigator, Mr. Chauvin.
Ottawa-Removal of snow, including Rideau Hall, $5,000.
How many men are employed in removing snow?
I could not tell exactly, but the number is a little larger than last year.
By whom are the men employed in removing snow recommended?
The men are engaged on the recommendation of any reputable person. Part of the work of removing snow is done by contract.
What is the explanation of the increase in the cost this year?

I suppose there are more buildings to attend to. I do not know of any other reason.
Ottawa-Repairs, including ventilation and lighting, furniture, &c., $250,000.
What has the minister to say about this item? The item for furniture was very severely criticised during the last parliament.

This vote is asked for the purpose of carrying out works of improvement, and repairing and procuring furniture. We find this necessary from time to time in order to maintain the public buildings in the city of Ottawa in a proper state of efficiency, and to meet the requirements of the public service. There is an increase from last year. The men who mainly perform these works are mechanics and labourers, employed under the direct supervision of the officers of the department, in compliance with requisitions received from the various departments.
When furniture is required by the department for the various buildings is it furnished by the department itself, or is it purchased outside?
As a general rule it is purchased outside. I do not think we manufacture furniture.
From what firm?

I really could not tell my hon. friend. It depends upon the kind of furniture that is required. I think that where a large purchase is contemplated, the purchase would have to be by contract. I have not had myself any transactions of the kind carried through since I have been in office. The demands have been limited to desks and things of that kind.
Has my hon. friend complied with the $5,000 limit in these cases?

In every instance.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On the Bill is printed, ' as reported by the Committee of the Whole.' It was not reported to the House, as the hour for private Bills having expired while the committee was sitting, it could not be reported.

Mr. CURRIE I do not go by anything that was expected or understood at the last meeting of the committee. I go by the order of proceedings as laid down in the order paper, anid item 41 says:
February 13-Further consideration in Com-mitte of the Whole of the following two Bills

And it names Bill (No. 16) and Bill (No. 84). I do not want to sultify the order paper, and I hold that the Bill is still in the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must rule that the Bill has passed the committee, because I was here waiting until the business of the Committee would be reported, but as the hour for private Bills expired before this Bill was reported, -although to any personal knowledge it had passed the committee and was ordered to be reported therefore I must treat it as reported now. There will be an opportunity for any motion or discussion on the third reading.
I happened to be out of the House when this Bill was last in committee, but I certainly want to oppose it.
I move that the Bill he now read the third time.

This Bill is for the renewal of a patent on wind-stackers, which the patentees have enjoyed the benefit of for 18 or 20 years. The patent covers a piece of machinery that is used on threshing machines in the western country and aha in other parts of Canada and in the whole world. I think in the interests of the consumer it is now time that such a patent should lapse. The effect of this would be a reduction in the cost of that piece of machinery of possibly a couple of hundred dollars.

I certainly think that the Bill should be allowed to stand, and be compelled to stand, especially as the hon. member who has charge of the Bill is not here. I called the attention of the House to these Bills when they first appeared. I said that they should be accompanied by an explanation of the specifications to prevent a fraud of any kind' on the public. No explanation has been given of what these patents cover, and this Bill is so framed that you cannot extract from it any idea of what the patent is. The hon. member for North York (Mr. Armstrong) took occasion to inquire at the Patent Office what the specifications of this patent were, and he received a letter from the Commissioner of Patents that the specifications would be sent to him for $6.50 or $7. Now, I think that the hon. member who desires to have the Bill read the third time, might just as well, in the 104
interest of peace, let it stand until we satisfy ourselves whether the patent deals with a stacking apparatus or not. I have never heard in the House an explanation of what the patent is. If the House does not adopt the rule that there should be such an explanation on every patent Bill, we shall have applications coming here for the renewal of the patent on the Bessemer process of making steel, and on a hundred other things, and the result will be that this country will be burdened down with patent rights which do not exist in other countries. We have stopped patent Bills before, alnd the people of Great Britain have been compelled to prevent the patenting of articles not patented in other countries. If a corporation has a patent such as this, it need not manufacture in Canada unless it likes. In view of these facts I think it would be well that the Bill should stand over; therefore, I object to the third reading at present.

The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples) is in error as to the facts connected with the Bill, which I excuse him for, as he has not been intimately associated with farming for many years. The hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) is, however, on a different footing; I think there is hot such an excuse for him. Had he been in this House when this Bill was passed by the committee last Tuesday, he would have known that the very explanation which he asks for was. then given. To correct first the hon. member for Macdonald, I may say that the patent does not cover anything with wind-stackers at all. The patent originally covered something connected with a fanning mill for cleaning grain. Just when the patent was taken out I cannot tell, but I know it was only a little over seven years ago. Mr. Wadge is the purchaser of the two patents. What the specifications cover I do not know, and it is not material to the Bill. Mr. Wadge purchased the patents in the ordinary way, on an 18 year basis; but owing to an error of his solicitors, who did not discover that the patent period paid for was only 6 years, he went on manufacturing, and has manufactured very largely ijn the city of Winnipeg, in the belief that he had the title for 18 years.
Is the patent in existence in any other country for this additional term or is it the fact that this six, or eight, or fourteen years required here does not hold good in the United States?
I do not think we are concerned with the United States?

Of course, the patent law of Canada states that when a patent



expires in the United States, it expires here automatically.

I could tell the House what I know about the patent law in a short time, I confess, to my hon. friend from North Simcoe. But, I know this, and it is sufficient for the present Bill, that Mr. Wadge, who purchased the patent, purchased the patent for Canada and that is all we are concerned with. The patent for Canada expired at the expiration of six years, although he had purchased it for 18 years. The reason that it expired was owing to an error of a firm of patent solicitors-a very competent firm-in the city of Winnipeg. In the spring of 1905 he began to manufacture this patent in Canada and he has'manufactured it continuously since. Last year he made 1,800 and this year expects to make 2,400 of the articles covered by the patent. This is simply to correct an error which was no fault of Mr. Wadge's, but only his misfortune. What is the result if we do not? In the first place, no one is injured if we do. This was all explained to the committee before and the House will forgive me if I traverse it again. The rights of all who may have acquired rights since the expiration of the patent are reserved in the Bill. Any rights acquired since the expiration of the patent are protected but Mr. 'Wadge's patent is continued to the expiration of the time he purchased it for. Had he known, which he did not, that it would expire at the end of six years, that being the only term that was paid for, he would have paid the very small fee and secured this renewal. This is simply to correct the most obvious of errors. It may be obtuseness on my part, but I cannot see why United States rights have anything to do with the Bill that is before the House.

It is quite natural that a man who is off the farm for a period becomes a little rusty in his farming pursuits. According to the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) the hon. member for Portage la Prairie has evidently become a little rusty in his law. However that may be, I frankly admit to the committee, according to the affidavit which I have now read and which was not brought to my attention before, the rights contained in this Bill do not extend as far as I thought they did. I thought the Bill renewed the patent for pneumatic stackers, and if such had been the fact I certainly would have opposed it. After hearing the explanation of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie I withdraw my protest against the Bill.
Motion agreed to. Bill read the third time, and passed.

House resumed in Committee of Supply.
Rideau Hall (including grounds)-improvements, furniture and maintenance, &c., $35,-
000.
Would the minister give an explanation of this item?

This vote is to be applied to carrying on the works of renewals, improvements and repairs, procuring furniture, &c., required for Rideau Hall, and maintaining the grounds in proper condition in accordance with the specifications of the chief architect. It is a smaller vote than last year.
I understand the vote is to complete the refurnishing of the interior of Rideau Hall. What will be the cost of that?

The cost was very considerable, amounting in respect of furniture and fittings to the sum of $5,000. The furniture was in a very poor state when the new government took office, and it was deemed absolutely necessary after an inspection to make this provision.

Is it the intention of the government to carry out the idea propounded by the late Governor General? Lord Grey was of opinion that the government should procure another site and build a new gubernatorial residence, in fact he had himself selected a piece of ground not far from Rideau Hall which was better suited for the purpose than the old estate. If I remember well, he had committed to his views gentlemen like the Prime Minister, and I believe also the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I remember being present last year at an afternoon tea when this question was discussed freely, and every one agreed that too much money had been spent on the old building and that there ought to be a new residence occupying another site.

I think the idea is a very-good one and ought to have been carried out. However, we have already made considerable expenditure for repairs. The cloak rooms have been built up, and other repairs carried out, and I do not think there is any immediate prospect of carrying out the project which nas been so often mooted. The residence was a wretched building for the purpose in the first place, and if some years ago a more suitable residence had been erected on a better site it would have been preferable to what has been done. The expenditure of large sums, however, has made the dwelling, I am informed, tolerably comfortable. And it will 1041
be suitable enough for the present. We have such large expenditures to make in the immediate future for departmental buildings, that until greater necessity arises I think we can leave the matter as it stands.
Dominion buildings-furniture, $19,000.
Is this vote for new furniture?

The vote is asked for the purchase of new furniture for the use of employees of the federal government in the Dominion buildings in the various provinces.
Power for running elevators, stamp cancelling machines, $35,000.
From whom do you get the power?
From the Ottawa Electric Company.

I take advantage of this opportunity to draw attention to a somewhat important matter. Not long ago-a friend of mime who is interested in a Canadian Coal Company, while visiting these-buildings suggested that there was no reason why heat, and power also, except such as that obtained by hydraulic means, for the public buildings of Canada might not be developed from the uise of Canadian coal. The coal at present used in our buildings is brought in from the United States, and although there may be some difficulties in the way, I would like to see the opportunity taken to assist Canadian industry. I draw the minister's attention to this point as perhaps it is one which he has so far overlooked. We all glory in Canadian made articles, and why should not Canadian coal be used in connection with the heating and lighting of our buildings in preference to coal from the United States. I do not know whether the minister has considered this question?
I have not.

Then I would like the minister to give the matter hiis at/tiem tion, because when we have a coal production in Canada of something lixe 10,000,000 tons, the least we can do in the way of rendering patriotic assistance to the men who produce that coal is to burn Canadian coal in our public buildings.

I have not had occasion to give this question very much consideration but it is certainly worthy of attention. I hope the time will come when we will be able to get all the heat we require through the medium of the immense water-powers-which surround this city.

Pending the time when we shall see the development of

electricity on such a large scale in this district, and the long expected ventilation of these buildings in a modern way such as the members of this House have been talking about for the last 30 years, I hope the minister will not lose sight of this important question of the use of Canadian coal in our public buildings. I ask the minister's serious attention to the matter-, and hope he will look into it.
Is the coal produced in the province from which my hon. friend comes suitable for heating purposes in buildings of this character?
Yes; people in the maritime provinces depend entirely upon the bituminous coal produced there for keeping their houses and buildings warm in winter.
Is it used in the government buildings in Halifax?

Yes, in the government buildings in the maritime provinces generally. The Minister of Public Works calls for tenders every year for the supply of coal for the public buildings in eastern Canada. There is no reason why he should not extend that so as to include the public buildings in central Canada as well. The coal from Alberta should be used, if it is not, as far east as Manitoba. Of course, the element of cost will enter into the question of supplying coal from the east and from the west for the central area; but, I submit, that every Canadian ought to be patriotic enough to prefer to have Canadian coal used in the public buildings, even if it costs a little more.
Did the late government do that?

This ' late ' government business is becoming a habit with my hon. friend from East Simeoe (Mr. Bennett). He is always looking to the past. We have a new government which came in with great professions of what they were going to do for Canada, particularly in such matters as this. We were told that if we ventured to buy or sell with the people of the United States, our loyalty would be endangered. I call the attention of the government which came in with these hopes and professions to an opportunity for action in line with those professions, and I hope they will not fail to act upon it at an early day.

All the same it must seem a little singular to people not familiar with political idiosyncrasies to find that the coal which is used this evening to heat this very building was bought outside of Canada to fulfil contracts made by the friends of the hon. member (Mr. Macdon-Mr. MACDONALD.
aid) in violation of the principle which he is so energetically defending to-night.
I decline to have a matter so serious as this dismissed by hon. gentlemen opposite with an excuse so hackneyed as the tu quoque argument. How long are they going to keep it uip?
Very long.

Then, I think the best thing they can do is to take up everything the late government did and imitate it. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) seems to forget the virtuous professions made on behalf of the party now in power of what they would do if they were given control of public affairs. But when we ask them to fulfil their pledges, even in a small degree, their answer is: We are not going to do it because you did not do it. 1 say we have had about enough of that proposition, if these gentlemen are to make any pretence whatever at standing to the principles. I am surprised specially at the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk). I have brought this question of the use of Canadian coal to his attention at the suggestion of a friend of his own. It is no answer to tell me that the liate government did not do it. The hon. minister ought to look into the matter. If there is good reason why Canadian coal should not be used in the public buildings, let us know it.

I have given the hon. member the assurance that I will look into the suggestion. But when he becomes irritated and indignant on this question of Canadian coal, I think it fair to remind him that the coal we are burning at this moment, and which, I think, was supplied under contract to the late government-I do not recollect giving any order for coal-was bought in contravention of the principle which the hon. gentleman laid down. We have had absolutely no opportunity of putting in practice the principle he is defending so valiantly; and, in answer to his indignant protests, it seams fair to say that that which excites his indignation was the act not of this government but of his friends.

If the hon. gentleman is worried because of any supposed indignation on my part, I Leg to assure him that I am in the best of humour. I accept the minister's assurance that he proposes to look into this .matter. If so, I hope that, if not this season then next session, we shall find that he has looked into the matter and has seen to it that Canadian coal iis purchased.

There seems to have been a very clear and decided difference between the attitude of hon. members on
the other side and that of the late govern-

ment in regard to these matters. It should be remembered that the late government was disposed toward freedom of trade with the United States, white oot friends opposite were very much opposed to it. What we are asking them to do is simply to live up to their professions. The fishermen in my county thought it would be a good thing if they were enabled to sell their fish in the United States. But a trooper representing the conservative party came down with a. poster ' Canada for the Canadians,' ' God save the King,' and so on, and the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite declared that it would be a bad thing to adopt the policy which the late government proposed. And now, when we ask the Minister of Public Works, in pursuance of the policy ot his party, to burn Canadian coal in the public buildings, his answer is that the late government did not do it. That is no proper answer. These gentlemen ought to be ready to live up to their professions, and one would think that to ask them to burn Canadian coal to heat the public buildings would be to call upon them to fulfil only a very small part of those professions. I notice by the public returns that Canada imported last year something like $50,000,000 worth of coal from the United States. I believe the greater part of that coal was burnt by those who were so much opposed to our doing business with the United States-by the combines, the railway magnates and the big manufacturers. Of course, if Nova Scotia could get a larger market in 'Canada for her coal it would be a good thing, and I would like to see everything done in that direction that we can do. I would like to see Nova Scotia coal go further west than it does at present. It is not sold much further west than Montreal. Could we sell it in Toronto and other places m Ontario, we should have a much larger business than we have at present. Anything this government could do to promote the consumption of our own coal would be but an attempt to live up to the professions they made >o,n September 21st.

I do not. know whether the suggestions of the hon. member for Pietou (Mr. Macdonald) are practical or not. But I would like to make a suggestion to the Minister of Public Works with reference to lighting the public buildings in Ontario. I would like him to take into considerationdhe fact that the Hydro-Electric Commission are doing a gTeat public service for Ontario, and as far as possible we should make use of the power they supply to light and heat the public buildings.
I will make a note of it, and when we take up the question of lighting I will look into the matter further.
I notice in this item a vote for ' Power for running elevators, stamp-cancelling machines, &c.' What are the stamp-cancelling machines?

A number of post offices have stamp cancelling machines, and they require electrical power to operate them.
Dominion Buildings-rente, $340,000.
Has the minister rented any new buildings since taking office?
I have rented one building on Metcalfe street since taking office. Last year the amount of our rentals was $306,485.89. This year we will require $340,000.
Are rentals cheaper or dearer this, year as compared with former years?
We are paying something like 98 cents or $1 a foot for the building on Metcalfe street, which is a somewhat high rental.
How much a foot was paid for the Woods building?
I think it is considerably more than that, but that was some years ago.
The minister mdans considerably less than $1 a foot, does he not?
No, I think it was more than $1 a foot in the case of the Woods building, but it would be difficult to establish any comparison because rents have gone up a great deal during the past few years.
My recollection is that the rent of the Woods building is less than 80 cents a foot.

That is one way of estimating rentals. We have found in the case of the last lease we made that we are paying 6 per cent upon the expenditure. I think in the case of the Woods building and other buildings rented at that time the percentage was far greater than that on the cost and that in some cases it went to 20 per cent.
What is the length of the lease of the Metcalfe street building?	[DOT]
Five years. I made that lease as short as possible, but I do not anticipate that we will be ready in five years, unless we use very great diligence, to install our departments at home.

Has the minister made any comparison between the rentals

paid by the departments and other people who rent buildings or does he find that the rentals paid by the government are just about the same, or sometimes less, than the rentals paid 'by other people?
I took the trouble to get special reports on that and I find that our rent is the same as that paid by other lessees in the locality.
What arrangement has the minister made in regard to lighting the building?

I am not in a position to give full information to the House in regard to lighting, but I have heard that there was a contract signed for a considerable space of time-four or five years- with the company that is at present lighting the building. I have not been able to verify that fact. The only thing that I have before me is the amount we ask to meet the requirements of lighting for the coming year. However, I intend to look into that as soon .as I have an opportunity to do so.
Does the contract require that the building is to be lighted by the government or by the owners?
We provide for the light if I am not mistaken.
Is it included in the $1 per foot?
I am under the impression, but I am not absolutely certain. The elevators are.
Have you a list of the new rentals?
The only new building rented by the government is this building on Metcalfe .street. They asked us $19,000, and we brought it down to $16,000. I think that we are paying $13,000.

If it is true that we are paying at the rate of $1 per foot for floor space in this new building, and that we rented the Woods building at 80 cents a foot, I would like to draw the fact to the attention of the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe). I would have expected to hear some protest from him when the rental is increased to such an alarming extent.

I do not know exactly what the conditions of our occupation of the Woods' building are. I think we heat that building. We do not heat the building we have rented o'n Metcalfe street, but, in any event, a comparison cannot be established on that footing at all. The increase in rentals within the past two or three years in Ottawa is something quite abnormal.
Mr. McKenzie. [DOT]
The real test in regard to the point raised by my hon. friend would be, what percentage does the proprietor receive upon his investment? Clearly, I think, there is no doubt that, in the case of the Woods' building, the percentage received by the proprietor far exceeded the sum of 15 per cent. In the case of the building rented on Metcalfe street the revenue of the proprietor does not exceed six per cent upon his investment. That is the proper test of what is a fair rental, because, in a city like Ottawa, or Montreal, where rents vary a great deal and increase in such a large proportion, you cannot say that $1 per foot at one period of time is a heavy rental when compared with a period four or five years previously, when the rentals were very low.

I suppose that if we are to make that the basis of the value of a building we must take the value of the building during the present year. Suppose that the owners of the Woods' building erected that building at a small cost twenty years ago and property has increased so that it is very valuable to-day, I do not think we should place the valuation altogether on the original capital that was put into the building. The same would be true of the Metcalfe street building if it were of any age. It would increase from year to year, as the city got larger.

The Woods' building was built especially for the government.
Mr. SINCLAIR-If we are to adopt that principle we should take the value of the building as it stands in the market to-day, and find out what the proceeds of that) value would be. That is what would be done in this case. If any one else were going to rent the building the proprietor would expect to get the value of his property as it stands in the market to-day, and not the value as represented by what he originally put into it.
Mr. MACDONALD-Are there any offers to rent buildings other than this one?

We are receiving offers every day. People imagine that we do not intend living in any other way. People come and offer buildings that they have on their hands, or offer to erect buildings suited exactly to our requirements provided we will pay the. rent. I think that condition of affairs is' regrettable, and that as soon as possible we should deal with the question.
What policy does the minister adopt in dealing -with these men who want to erect buildings for the government?

My policy at the present time is, in spite of the discomfort and want of accommodation that we are undergoing everywhere, to try and rent as little

as possible and push as quickly as possible the adoption of some comprehensive scheme ' for erecting buildings of our own and getting out of these rented buildings.
Does the minister contemplate renting any additional buildings at the present time?
I am afraid that before we are in a position to get into our own departmental building we will require further accommodation. ,
For what departments?

All the departments seem to be in want of further accommodation. Many departments are divided up in different parts of the city and they complain a great deal of the inconvenience that it causes them. Some departments are unduly congested and cannot accommodate their staff. They are prevented from securing the necessary help for the work of the departments not because they have not money to pay the employees but because they have no accommodation for them.
I suppose the buildings for the departments are scarce?

Yes.
Dominion buildings-salaries of caretakers, etc., $250,000.
Would the minister permit this item to stand as there are some returns which are coming down and I would like him to hold it over until we get them?

There is no objection excepting that we will have further items in the supplementary estimates which will enable the question of caretakers to be discussed and I am very anxious, if possible, with the indulgence of the committee, to get rid of the main estimates to-night and allow the committee to take up the items on some other department.
This will be the only item that we will ask to be held over.

I call the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the salaries paid to the caretakers of public buildings in Nova Scotia, and while I do not know how they compare with the salaries paid to similar officials in the other provinces, I submit that the salaries in Nova Scotia are altogether too low for a living wage. It is not hard work, but it takes all the time of the caretaker from early morning till late at night. In eastern Nova Scotia the mails arrive sometimes at midnight and at four o'clock in the morning and the caretaker must be there to receive them if the nost office happens to 'be in the public building. A salary of $400 such
as is paid in these places is not sufficient to support a man and his family. I should think it ought to be $600 or $650 to the man whose whole time is taken up in any. government service especially, as of late years, the cost of living has gone up to such an extent.

The salaries paid to caretakers in Nova Scotia appear to range from a minimum of $400 to $770, whereas in Quebec, except in Montreal where they are $500 and $600 the salaries range from $150 to $300. There is $150 paid in Laprairie, $300 at Longueuil, $300 at L'Assumption, $150 at Hull. There appears to be no disproportion between the salaries of caretakers cf public buildings in Nova Scotia and in the other provinces, but I will make a note of the remarks of the hon. gentleman, and inquire into the matter.
Water supply-$28,000.

Last year, Dr. Black, then member for Hants, called special attention on several occasions to the water supply furnished to the public buildings by the city of Ottawa, and as Dr. Black is not here this session the matter is not engaging the attention it deserves. The Minister of Public Works will remember the epidemic of typhoid we had in the city last, year, and I think it was the present Speaker of the House who suggested that parliament should be prorogued or adjourned for a period rather than that the members of the House should take the tremendous risk of drinking the water we had to drink in this city last year. That epidemic has passed, and I fear there will be very little done to improve the water of the city until we are in the throes of another epidemic. The government pays large sums of money towards the upkeep of municipal work in Ottawa, and as the representatives of the people are bound to come here, they should feel that they are as safe in this city as anywhere in Canada, and that they are not forced to drink water which may bring disease and possibly death. I have remarked nothing in the proceedings of the city council which would conduce to bring about a better state of affairs in this respect than we had last year. I think the Minister of Public Works should refuse positively to contribute any money from the treasury of Canada to the upkeep or beautifying of the city of Ottawa until there is a pure water supply in the city. Nothing will bring people to their senses like stopping the money supply, and as long as the city of Ottawa is getting the money of the country without any protest it is not likely that anything will be done. It is quite within the power of the city of Ottawa to give us a supply of pure water. The minister should say to the city authorities that they will not get any more money from us until they put themselves

in a position to deserve that treatment from the government. I bring this matter most seriously to the notice of the minister.

I am afraid I cannot take the rigid position which my hon. friend has suggested, and refuse to pay for any water until I have an absolute certainty that the water is pure. The subject is a very interesting one, and so far as we can help to solve the water problem in Ottawa or anywhere else we will do the best we can as a government. I think I have in the department a full and interesting report on the water conditions in Ottawa, and if so I shall lay it on the table of the House.
What truth is there in the report published in the press that the Minister of Public Works has signed a contract for the St. John harbour works?

The fact is not as alleged. There is no contract signed yet, but we intend carrying out the improvements contemplated at Courtenay Bay on the east side of the harbour of St. John, as soon as I have the necessary authority to enter into that contract.
Graving dock, $35,000.

There are rumours afloat that the Levis graving dock will be enlarged or that a new dock may be built.
If I remember well, there was formed a year ago, a company composed of Sir Montague Allan and other gentlemen of very high repute, and they asked the government for the usual subsidy, but owing to some difference between them and the government as to the amount to be guaranteed, the project fell through. I see by the papers in Quebec that a delegation from that city is to meet the Prime Minister and the Minister oi Public Works shortly, and that one of the questions to be discussed is that of a new dock in Quebec. Will my hon. friend state whether tlie dock to be built in Quebec will be built by a company under the Dry Docks Subsidy Act, or built by the government? In Quebec the opinion generally expressed is that the government should build the dock and operate it. On the other hand, there are people who think that it should be in the hands of a company, i have no opinion to express myself, but I would like to know wliat is the policy of my hon. friend. It is stated in ' L'Evenement ' that this meeting is to be strictly private, only a select few to be present; but this is a matter of vital concern to the whole country, and I would like to know whether the hon. gentleman will receive suggestions only from this Quebec delegation. Many people believe that a graving dock at Quebec is a national necessity; many believe Mr. MeKENZIE.
that the harbour of Quebec is superior to all our other harbours. I regret to see that neither the hon. Postmaster General or any of the Quebec members are present, but I know that they -axe very optimistic with reference to the future of Quebec, and I would like to have an expression of their views on this question. I hope the hon. minister will give us a peep into his department, and let us see what his policy is in regard to it.

The question is a very large one to discuss at this point, but there is no doubt that there exists at Quebec a great necessity for a suitable graving dock. No port anywhere nowadays is complete without a graving dock. European ports, which have cost anywhere from fifty to a hundred million dollars invariably have graving docks, and the same is true of properly equipped ports according to modern notions in the United States and in South America. Quebec is one of the ports recommended by the Transportation Commission to be improved as a national port. There is a graving dock there which I visited some time ago, and while I was convinced that a graving dock there could be made a paying concern, the existing one is too small for modern requirements and it has never been administered in such a way as to pay, although it yields a fair revenue. Another, and large dock, is an absolute necessity if Quebec is to be equipped as a national port. Nothing has been done for that port during the last few years. No equipment of any serious and durable value has been carried out under a general scheme of improvement. Such a general scheme or plan is the first step to be taken. It is the first step we took in Montreal under somewhat different conditions, and even though we had there a plan which would take years to carry out fully, the equipment of the port of Montreal is at present very far from complete. The policy of the late government was to grant subsidies, under the legislation of 1908 and 1910, to companies for graving docks. I do not think it is a bad system, but the legislation requires to be improved in many respects. I am not. prepared to say that the government should undertake, in all the 12 or 13 national ports of this country, the construction of graving docks; but the necessity of an improved graving dock at Quebec, in keeping with modern requirements, is apparent, and as soon as possible that matter will be taken up.

We are all familiar with the legislation of 1910, and previous legislation to stimulate the construction of dry-docks. In connection with that legislation several projects were mentioned, at Collingwood, St. John and other points.

The provisions of the legislation were that if a dry-dock of a certain character were constructed, a subsidy, proportionate to the cost, would be given. The first legislation failed to bring about any results, and amendments were made increasing the subsidies. My purpose in calling attention to this is to make an inquiry of my bon. friend in respect to the St. John dry-dock. An appropriation was made recently by this House for improvements at Courtenay Bay at St. Jlohn, and since then I understand that tenders were invited for the construction with the terminals at Courtenay Bay, for a breakwater for the protection of that portion of the harbour of St. John which is exposed to south-easterly gales, and for dredging that portion of the harbour.
Tenders for all these works were invited en bloc, but any one who desired to bid for other portions of the work would necessarily have to include in their tenders an offer to construct a dry dock. Tenders were received and I understand the contract has been awarded, but it would not be opportune nor relevant for me at present to criticise in any way the course taken either by the present government or its predecessors. I do not desire at present to criticise any action that has been taken, however much I might be disposed under proper circumstances to do so. The firm which holds the contract for the construction of these several works, will, I assume construct a dry dock. Will they be entitled to receive any consideration as a firmi under the subsidy Act, or is the work to he constructed and paid for by the government and owned and operated by it when completed, entirely apart from any consideration under the Act now in force?

I am glad: that the hon. gentleman narrowed his question down to the one he has just put, because the general question of the improvement of St. John harbour would require extensive application. Therefore I will simply answer him by saying that the tenderer for the work obliges himself to build a dry dock at St. John and nothing more. It is as if he had applied for the subsidy under the terms of the Subsidy Act of 1910, and after the proper formalities have been complied with, the works will become entitled to the ordinary subsidy as defined by the Act. The government will not own the dock. It will be the property of the party who constructed it just as in ordinary cases and that party will be entitled to the subsidy. The reason of this is that it was not supposed that we could get anybody to undertake the risk of constructing a dry dock in St. John except under the conditions of that person having the contract for the construction of the other works referred to in the tender. My hon. friend understands, I hope, that it is' absolutely a construction
under the ordinary conditions of the Dry Docks Act.

Would I be correct in understanding the minister to state that when the contract of the Messrs Griffiths is completed, they will naturally receive the compensation under that contract, and the government will naturally have paid for the construction of a dry dock as well as for the other works contemplated under the contract?

No, my hon. friend is mistaken as to that. It is not a block contract such as my hon. friend stated. There is no contract as yet. It is contemplated to make a contract with unit prices and details, but it does not enter into the sum we mentioned in the contract price of the dry dock. The condition was that they would execute the work, and furthermore oblige themselves to build a dock under the Dry Dock Act.

Then my hon. friend having stated that it would be impossible to secure a dry dock under the subsidy Act at St. John, apart from the consideration of these other works, it is to be assumed that the contractor will perform these several works- that is the construction of a breakwater, the dredging of a harbour, and the construction of the docks-for a certain sum of money aalculated of course upon the schedule prices? Is it not also to be inferred that the government will have paid them not only for these several works, but in addition have given them in the prices awarded, a contribution to the construction of a dry dock? That would be the inference-that apart from the amount of money which he had received for the construction of these other works, they would not be willing to construct a dry dock under the terms of the Dry Docks Subsidy Act. That seems to me quite apparent. It may be all right-I am not going to question it at this moment, it would not be proper for me to do so-but I simply want to understand the situation; and therefore while we know as to the cost of the several dry docks which may have been built in Canada, on the Pacific coast or on the great lakes, under the terms of the Subsidy Act, in the case of St. John we do not know, because a portion of the consideration for the construction of that dry dock is involved in the construction of the breakwater, the dredging of the harbour, and the construction of the loading docks known as the terminals. That would seem to be the clear reasoning to be gathered from the circumstances as detailed by my hon. friend. I do not quite so understand it.

My hon. friend has made a natural inference, but be is entirely^ misr taken. No doubt the House will desire to see the contract when it is prepared so as

to examine the unit prices in order to convince itself that the dry dock it not at all provided for hy the consideration therein, and the inference of my bon. friend is very natural until one has occasion to look into the details of the contract. The situation is this:	It was deemed! impossible
to induce anybody with a harbour such as St. John, unimproved, possessing no equipment of a modern kind whatever, to undertake the icomstnuction of the dry dock there; but when these works of importance will have been carried out, the shipping will undoubtedly greatly increase, and with a harbour properly equipped under the terms of this arrangement there will be a better prospect of a dry dock. Therefore it was deemed necessary, I think very wisely, to include in the contract with a large and powerful firm, the stipulation that when these works of improvement had been carried out, a dry dock would be constructed. But my hon. friend bears in mind, no doubt, that when the time comes for constructing that dry dock an estimate of the cost of it will have to be laid before the government and carefully gone into by its engineers in order to determine what subsidies will be paid to the company. When this estimate is fully gone into, and when the unit prices mentioned in detail in the contract is considered, it will be seen that the natural inference of my hon. friend is absolutely not founded.

If my hon. friend is correct and the works are not to he carried on contemporaneously, then I can see some reason for the action taken.
