Apart from that, it seems to me that no concern in Canada would compete for the several V'orks in connection with the harbour terminals, if associated with that work there was required to be an undertaking to engage in the construction of a dry dock even at a later date. That is to say that practically, if not wholly, it prevents competition in the dredging, the breakwater, and in the terminal docks so far as Canadian contractors are concerned.

My hon. friend knows that the form of tender was established before this government came into office. I have examined it very carefully. I find the tenders that are in greatly reduced the price, as the House will see when the matters come before it. But I cannot find fault with the form of the tenders; I think it was a good form in every respect.
I understand that the part tendered for by Norton, Griffiths & Co., has been awarded.
No, there has been no award of any kind.
No partial award?
No, there will be no partial award. The whole work will be undertaken ' en bloc '.
Referring to the Quebec proposed dry-dock, has the minister received any offer from a syndicate or a company which would undertake the construction of the new grading dock at Levis?
There is no proposition now for either Levis or Quebec before the government.

I am told that a syndicate has been formed in Quebec and that it has already had some interviews with the minister, with a view to obtaining a subsidy or guarantee from the government in connection with the construction of a graving dock at Levis.

I have no knowledge of that. I saw some gentlemen to-day who are interested in some such construction and who made some representations to me in reference to the Subsidy Act of 1910, which requires amendment in several particulars, and they laid their observations before me. Whether these gentlemen constitute a syndicate or not, or what they intend, I have no knowledge.
Would the hon. gentleman have any objections to giving the names of the gentlemen who interviewed him?

I do not know if my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) is right in calling them a ' syndicate '. Mr. Webster, of the Quebec Harbour Board saw me in reference generally to the very urgent improvements required in thp port of Quebec. With him was a gentleman whose name I do not remember, who seemed to be very much interested in dry-docks, and a couple of members of the district. Sir Rodolphe Forget was also of the number. They made representations merely with reference to the Quebec harbour improvements and the necessity of enlarging the scope of the Dry-dock Act. No mentipn was made of any particular scheme.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say that the tenders put in were at lower prices. Does he mean to say that there has been an actual reduction in the prices, or has the change in the specifications meant that the total, as his engineers figure it out, will be a reduction in the cost of the work?

I meant a general reduction, calling at the same time for lower prices. The tenders are all very high. The department did not think it would be possible to recommend the adoption of even the lowest tender unless it was possible to bring the lowest tenderer within

a more measurable distance of the estimate. That was what I alluded to.
As I understand it, the Department of Public Works has nothing to do with the dry-dock at Montreal.
We have everything to do with it.
I thought it was under the supervision of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Under the Dry-Dock Subsidy Act, all dry-docks subsidized are constructed under the Department of Public Works.
Yes, but I understood that arrangements had been made between Vickers Maxim and the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal.

There have been various contracts and arrangements between the Harbour Commissioners and Vickers Maxim who are constructing a floating dock; but the determination of the subsidy and the class of floating dock came under the consideration of my department before my time. The documents are all in my department.
I understand that before the department pays over the subsidy the work will be inspected. I understood that the builders had made arrangements with the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal.

I cannot speak with absolute knowledge as to that. I believe so, and all these arrangements would come under the purview of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. There may have been some sales or leases of land or contracts for the preparation of the cradle of the floating-dock. Where we come in is the determination of the subsidy, the inspection of the work and the approval of the plans.

There are rumours about a sale of land. The hon. gentleman ought to know that no lands "were sold to the company but that the arrangement made with the Harbour Board of Montreal is with relation to the lands which are being dredged by the company; but they have had no sales of land from the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal.

When I say ' Sale of land,' they must have come to an arrangement with the Harbour Commissioners as to where they would install the floating dock and must have concluded a lease or alienation of some kind in order to have a place within the limits of the harbour of Montreal.
No, the hon. gentleman is not right in that. I say that with all due respect. I would like to make that point very clear in order to dispel the rumours afloat.
What rumours?
The rumours which the hon. gentlemen probably knows.
I have not heard any.

The Harbour Commissioners of Montreal have made arrangements with Vickers Maxim that the material dredged out of the river St. Lawrence over a long distance will be used by the Vickers Maxim Company for their plant. But there has been no land on the main shore sold to the company.
I know nothing of that.
I am very glad the hon. gentleman states that. Has he any idea when the dock will be completed?

I have heard a rumour that it is nearly finished. It is being constructed in the old country and is to come out to us in the spring. It is a floating dock. The cradle, or place where it is to be put is at the foot of the harbour of Montreal, and I imagine the dock will be installed there about the month of June.
Public Works-chargeable co collection of revenue-telegraph lines-land and cable telegraph lines, lower St. Lawrence and maritime provinces, including working expenses of vessels required for cable services, $140,-
000.

Has my hon. friend looked into the case of the Magdalen Islands cable linking the islands with the mainland? Fot several months in the year these people -are cut off, and I obtained several years ago the advantage of a cable line and a -cheap rate. I would like to know if the rate is being maintained or if it h-as been changed?

I do not think there has been any change.
Mr. M-cKENZIE. Referring to the item including the working -expenses of vessels required for cable service, have you more than one vessel, -o-r is the ' Tyrian- ' the only vessel?
I think so.

Som-e two years ago the head-quarters of this vessel, the ' Tyrian,' was moved from Halifax to North Sydney. The m-ost of the work performed by this boat is in the Gulf and River St. Lawrence, and it was -considered that North Sydney was a -central place for the homes of the crew, and -also a pliac-e -at whi-ch co-al could -be obtained -more economically and conveniently than Halifax. I am told

lately, although not departmentally, that this vessel has been moved back to Halifax. Would the minister tell me anything about this?

As far as I know the ' Tyrian ' was moved to Halifax before the 21st of September last. I think that at present the vessel is at Dartmouth or Halifax and there has been no change since the government came into power.
Telegraph lines-Yukon system (Ashcroft-Dawson), $213,000.
Is that for maintenance?
No, this is for some very important extensions. We expect to have a revenue this year from our telegraph lines of $110,000.
Has my hon. friend any idea what rate the people pay, or is it the rate of the ordinary telegraph lines?

I think it is the same rate as that of the ordinary telegraph lines.
Telegraph service generally, $7,000.
What is that item for?

That item is to be applied to cover a number of unavoidable expenditures in connection with the Dominion telegraph service, including Point Pelee telegraph line service, superintendent, repairs, operators, use of instruments, travelling expenses, and stationery. The appropriation for 1911 was $7,000 and the expenditure from the 1st of April, 1910, to the 28th of February, 1911, was $5,548. A request has been made to keep in abeyance the item under Dominion buildings, salaries of caretakers. There is no special objection to that except that if my hon friends would [DOT]allow that item to pass it would enable us to take away a large quantity of documents required in the department and questions which might he raised under the item can be brought up under several items of the supply estimates. It will be a convenience to the department if the committee will adopt that item completely, which would close the main estimates in so far ias the Department of Public Works is concerned.

Unfortunately, I was not in a few moments ago and perhaps the minister would let me know something in regard to the item for telegraph lines between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. Has the minister received any request from the Maritime Telephone Company which has telephonic communication with the island in regard to assisting their project in substitution of the old agreement which was made with the Anglo-American Cable Co.? I understand that they are prepared to give a better service. I am surprised that our friends from Prince Mr. McKENZIE.
Edward Islland are not here to refer to the matter. I understand that the Maritime Telephone Company are making some representations in regard to the matter. Does the minister recall anything in regard to it?

Application was made quite recently by the Telephone Company of the maritime provinces to us to lay a cable to the island. The matter was considered and we came to the conclusion, as far as I can recollect that we could not do it.

Of course the matter is one in which the people of the island are primarily interested. There is a long standing complaint in regard to the lack of accommodation furnished by the Anglo-American Cable Company, which has some old contract, and I assume that that may be the difficulty that the minister anticipates in connection with this matter.
Is there any telephone communication at the present time?

Yes there is. The reason I speak of the matter is because there is an island midway between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, which is in my county, which this present telephone service touches, which is inhabited by quite a number of people, and which is a very fertile place. I understand that the company were making some application to the government-I do not know exactly what the nature of it is-but I should hope that the minister would be able to find some method of dealing with it which would give a better service than that which is obtained under the vote which, I think, is one which is given to the Anglo-American Cable Com pany. It formerly was impossible to have a. telegram delivered in Pri,nce Edward Island after eight o'clock at night, owing to some regulation of the cable company. If that financial assistance were diverted to the telephone people, the whole of the maritime provinces would be benefited. I hope the minister has not fully closed the door against considering the proposal that these maritime province people have submitted and if the minister could see his way clear -having regard to existing contracts to make any arrangement with them, it would be much to the public advantage.

There is quite a recent application-I do not remember the circumstances very well, but I would be very glad to show the file and correspondence to anybody who is interested in the subject. 1 was impressed with the idea that they were asking the government to lay a telephone cable largely for the benefit of the telephone company in question. It may be that there is some public interest operating in favour of our laying the cable between the mainland and the island, but at the time it seemed

to me that we were invited to render this service to a private corporation. II I am mistaken in that I shall be very glad to look into it again.
Of course, at the present time the service is performed not by the government but by a private corporation, which is not locally interested, and does not attempt to serve local interests.
They have a monopoly.

They have a monopoly, as my right hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) .states. There is this consideration, that the government do grant assistance to private companies and if this company of local people were to undertake the service the minister might be asisured that it would be very much improved.
Calculations were made in my presence that it was a considerable expenditure from which we did not appear to stand to derive any revenue.

There have been telephone companies formed of late in the peninsula of Gaspe, and when they came to provide for putting up their lines they found that the distances, were so great and the patrons so few that it was very difficult for them to find money sufficient to erect the poles. I understand they intend to ask the Minister of Public Works for permission to use these telegraph poles to string their wires on. The settlements are very scattered around that peninsula, and the telephone has become such a modern necessity that I hope the Minister of Public Works will be generous when applications of this kind are made to him. I trust he will allow the telephone companies in such a remote region as that to string their wires on the government telegraph poles.

In these sparsely settled regions I think it is a good policy for the government as far as possible to grant the right to telephone companies, under certain circumstances, to string their wires along our poles. We have had no applications so far, but I would be inclined to favour the idea, provided the public interests b|e safeguarded. Of course, unless there are very special circumstances it is a bad principle to follow.
Immigration-salaries, agencies, in Canada, Cfreat Britain and Foreign countries, $400,000.	I .	.	;	.

Has the government settled upon any immigration policy for the maritime provinces? The subject was discussed here some few weeks ago in the House, and I would like to
know if the minister or the government has arrived at any matured plan.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have had a deputation wait on me from New Brunswick, in the person of the Premier and Mr. Grimmer, and one other of their colleagues, and we discussed a proposition suitable to that province, and which appeared satisfactory to them. With regard to Nova Scotia, I had the pleasure of being waited upon by a large deputation, the spokesman of which was Mr. Cummings, a government official of that province, and we discussed a plan which was apparently satisfactory to them, and which included the appointment of one or two agents in London to work together with our own staff in European countries, and the appointment also of one or two agents in the province of Nova Scotia.
Was Mr. Cummings delegated by the government of Nova Scotia to interview the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think he so represented himself.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I think Mr. Messenger was appointed by a farmers' meeting in the province to meet the minister, and Mr. Cummings happened to be here and went along.
About what date did the department engage the services of Mr. Hawkes, and was he promised the position prior to the last election in the event of the defeat of the Liberal government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I may tell my hon. friend that the matter of Mr. Hawkes' appointment was never discussed previous to the election, so far as I know. In fact it was my own suggestion to Mr. Hawkes, probably a month or more after the election, that he should undertake this work.
Would the minister give us a statement in regard to the officers in Great Britain and the Uunited States?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In May, 1911, A. F. Jury was transferred, from Liverpool to Exeter, succeeding Mr. Alex. McOwan, who resigned on the 1st March, 1911, John Mclennan was transferred from Aberdeen to Liverpool, and G. H. Mitchell was transferred from Birmingham to the High Commissioner's office in London; J. K. Millar, formerly of Saltcoats, Sask., was appointed Agent at Birmingham. W. B. Cumming, formerly of Saskatoon, Sask., was appointed Agent at Aberdeen, Scotland.
In the United States, J. S. Crawford was transferred from Kansas city, Mo., to Syracuse, N. Y. in January, 1911; W. H. Rogers from Indianapolis, Ind., to Kansas city, Mo., March, 1911: George Aird appointed agent ait Indianapolis,

March, 1911, and in January, 1912, Mr. R. A. Garrett, of Manitou, Man., was
appointed acting agent in charge of the office in St. Paul, Minn., relieving Mr. E. T. Holmes, who is seriously ill. No new offices have been established in Great Britain. No office is closed in the United States except the one in Boston for reasons which my hon. friend can appreciate. We have established offices in the United States at Crookston and Des Moines, Iowa.
Who are in charge of these two offices?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Askett at Crookston and Mr. Black at Des Moines.

In regard to the appointment of Mr. Hawkes, who has been touring England at the expense of Canada and writing flamboyant articles about himself and sending cables to Canada about his activities over there, I do not know whether the minister promised this gentleman his position during the last election campaign or not. I had the honour of a visit from Mr. Hawkes in my constituency, where he undertook to instruct the men who nad come from old England and Scotland as to their duty in regard to political matters in this country. I am glad to say my constituents had the good sense to resent the attempts of this gentleman, who had hardly reached the standard that he could call himself a dignified Canadian, to direct them how to vote in the somewhat eggressive manner in which he did. I am sorry my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) is not here so that he might tell the minister of the performance which his appointee indulged in in his county when the hon. member had to apologize for his utterances and his conduct in discussing public questions.
I do not know whether the minister saw the very keen review and discussion of Mr. Hawkes made by the Victoria ' Sunset.' It does seem to me on general principles that a man who goes forth to represent this country, in immigration matters or anything else, should stop talking about having been born in Scotland or England or anywhere else-that he should be a Canadian first, last and always, and should go forth in that capacity. But that does not seem to be the method of this electioneering agent of my hon. friend or of some of his friends. The performances of Mr. Hawkes are not such as to bring very much pride to the average Canadian who is proud of his country. From what I saw and heard of him in the maritime provinces in the last election, I am surprised at the minister, who is usually given the credit of being a man of sound judgment, selecting a man like Mr. Hawkes, who seems to be running Mr. ROGERS.
papers for his own glorification. I saw in Montreal the other day the British ' News/ which is his newspaper, and which contains quotations from his own speeches delivered in the old country, and writings as to his various performances. You would think that he was the centre of interest for the whole of Canada from the very hour he arrived in Great Britain, and that nobody else who had ever gone there before knew anything about Canada. It seems to me that the minister should send for that gentleman and give him a lecture as to his performances instead of attempting to foist him on the Canadian people.
' Mr. ROGERS. I have not had the privilege of reading any of the articles to which my hon. friend refers, but I am informed, and I believe correctly informed, that Mr. Hawkes has now no interest whatever in the British ' News/ or whatever the name of the paper is. I regret that Mr. Hawkes met with such misfortune in the maritime provinces on the occasion to which my hon. friend refers; but I am glad to say that he had not the same misfortune in other provinces which he visited about that time. However, that had nothing to do with the appointment which he at present holds, further than this, that I recognized in Mr. Hawkes a . suitable man for the work of immigration, in bringing to the notice of the people of England, Scotland and Ireland the great advantages of Canada for immigrants. I think still that Mr. Hawkes is a desirable man for that work, and from the statements of my hon. friend, he is-evidently a man capable of securing a good deal of advertising

He advertised himself.
Mr. ROGERS

and that is the right
sort of man as an immigrant agent. I may say, with regard to bringing Mr. Hawkes back from the old country, that I believe he is on the ocean now, and he will be here in a few days.
Will his mission be completed then?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is not engaged for any definite period. That will be determined when we get his report.
What is his work for the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
His work was first of all going to the different provinces of Canada with the view of enlisting the co-operation of the local governments with the Dominion in the matter of a general immigration policy. He visited all the local governments with a good deal of

success. Then he went to London for the purpose of visiting our different agencies and offices there, in order to make a report as to whether or not it would be advisable to make any change. I hope we shall have his report in a few days after he arrives, and I shall be glad to submit it to my hon. friends for their consideration.
Could not that work have been done by somebody else in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I regarded Mr. Hawkes
as a very suitable man for this work, arid he has certainly done it very well up to date.

Were any definite arrangements of a lasting character made between the department of the hon. minister and the government of Nova Scotia, for instance, with regard to immigration? What does the hon. gentleman mean by saying that this gentleman met with considerable success?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He met with success in interviewing the government of British Columbia, and I believe he met with the same success with the government of Alberta. I have had a letter, I think, from a member of every local government in the Dominion of Canada, after Mr. Hawkes' visit, expressing satisfaction with the idea of their cooperating with us in immigration work.
That was not a new idea in this country.
It was not Mr.'; Hawkes' idea.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, it is our own. idea.
What credit is he to get for it?'

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He was selected as the man to have the interviews and to arrange the plan of co-operation with each province as far as we possibly could. Take the province of Ontario:	We are combining our
forces and saving a considerable amount of money instead of duplicating our work. The same applies to New Brunswick, and it was only a few days ago that I had a report from a member of the government of Nova Scotia, shortly after Mr. Hawkes had visited that province, and we had the deputation the other day with regard to cooperation in an immigration policy suitable to that particular province.

That is a tribute to my hon. friend's judgment, if the idea had not existed before, that it would be a good thing to co-operate with the provinces. My hon. friend is altogether too modest. Be need not fancy that Mr. Hawkes is of [DOT] some consequence because the minister conceived the idea and Mr. Hawkes was sent to_ carry it out. I am satisfied that the minister had in the department men of experience, whose knowledge of this whole immigration business would have enabled them to carry out the minister's idea better than Mr. Hawkes. The minister is adroitly confusing the fact that he conceived this idea with the notion that that is a defence of Mr. Hawkes. A man who had hardly any root in this Canadian soil, was hardly the man to send forth with all the panoply of the greatness attributed to him in his own newspapers, for this work. The cablegrams about his movements in the old country are sent by himself, and of course the government pays for them. I am quite sure that the hon. minister has gentleman in his department who could have done more effective work. From what we have seen of Mr. Hawkes in this country, he is not a man who should be sent abroad bearing any credentials from this government as a sample Canadian agent. The minister is putting forward his idea of co-operation as if it were some defence of Mr. Hawkes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid that my hon. friend is not acquainted with Mr. Hawkes, or he would not have made such a statement. Mr. Hawkes has spent years in western Canada, and he knows our conditions as few men do, so that I felt that he was a suitable man for the work. While we have first-class men in the Immigration Department, every man there has a special work of his own, and it was necessary to have some one else, and I selected Mr. Hawkes as a suitable man to stir up interest in immigration.

Mr. Hawkes was given the work of interviewing the various provincial governments and formulating with them a policy of co-opeTation in immigration. My hon. friend has told us that. I think that he should give us some idea of what the proposition iis in regard to each of the provinces. While there has been some co-operation in the past, I understand from what the hon. minister says that it is intended to adopt the principle of co-operation as an important part of our immigration policy from this time forward. That policy having been decided on, Mr. Hawkes the special agent of the government, having interviewed the governments of the different provinces, and amicable arrangements, we are informed, having been arrived at, I think the minister should give us an idea of what those arrangements are, so that the House may judge of the merits of the scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
With certain of the provinces who have agents as we have had in the past, and as we have in London, we are uniting the offices, in so far as we pos-

sibly can, and are working from the same office, instead of having dual work. As between the Dominion and a particular province, we are working and co-operating together to that extent. No'w, Mr. Hawkes will be here in a few days. He left rather hurriedly for London about Christmas time without presenting his report on his tour of inspection through the different provinces of Canada. However, the report will be prepared by the time he returns here, and I will be nleased to present it to. the House in order that the full details may be gleaned as to his work. -

I am very much interested in this work which Mr. Hawkes is carrying on. I do not know whether the government has had a report from that gentleman of an interview which he apparently has had with the representatives of the province of Quebec, which province within the past few months has established in London a new agency. It was a new departure and one which has been much commented on by the people of Quebec. I should be very pleased to learn that Quebec's agent in London is working in cooperation with the officers of the Department of the Interior. Speaking with regard to the province of Quebec, and the immigration policy as it affects that province-and not only Quebec, but the Dominion as a whole-I know that necessarily the immigration from Europe must above all come from the British Isles. I favouT that policy, and I believe it to he ia wise and good one. Of course we get good citizens from the continent of Europe, and we make good Canadians of them. That has been seen in the mixed population of the west where the foreign element has been quietly absorbed and to-day forms some of our best citizens. The minister himself, born and bred as he was in the province of Quebec, and being one of its bright sons, is aware that his native province has sent thousands of her sons into the maritime provinces, over hundreds of thousands into the province of Ontario, and many thousands into the far west; and he will admit that the province of Quebec deserves to be helped somewhat by a slight sprinkling of French emigration from Belgium and from France I have given this question some consideration for years past. At the request of myself and some of my colleagues in the late government we obtained from his predecessors the appointment of agents in Belgium, and in France. An announcement recently appeared in the press that the salaries of the agents in France had been cut off. I do not believe that statement was true, and I am glad to see my hon. friend take exception to it. It would be a very unjust proceeding if that were done because the men who represent the de-Mr. ROGERS.
partments in Paris, Mr. Wiallard and his assistants, are very able and active, and they have become experts in the matter of French immigration. The minister knows that it is very difficult for a Canadian agent, or indeed for any agent, to make any headway in France, as regards emigration to this country. The French government is opposed to emigration and they have very many good reason for that attitude. They have a standing army and compulsory military service, they have their own colonies, and more than that, lacking the virtues of their descendents in New France . they	lose in	natural
growth of population thousands of citizens. Naturally the government of France is not favourably disposed towards emigration, in fact it adopts many precautions to prevent it. Yet there are a certain number of people in France who are prepared, of their own volition to emigrate to this continent, and among that class our agents are quite able to get their proper share for this country. Many of these French immigrants go to Argentina and the United States. During the last fifteen years we have received our fair quota but we could find room for more. We must always remember that it is very difficult for our agents to make any active propaganda in the various provinces of France, in fact some years ago the then Prime Minister, Mr. Clemenceau, .issued an edict or circular, prohibiting agents from conducting any active 'propaganda in the interests of emigration to this country. I read that circular myself, being in France at the time of the death of the late Mr. Prefontaine, and I saw Mr. Clemenceau who was then the Minister of the Interior. He explained to me the reasons which 1 gave a moment ago, that they could not see their way to facilitate the activities of our agents. However, he said, out of the people who did go abroad they were quite satisfied that the Canadians should get their fair share. As regards the Belgians that country is small in extent but numerously populated, and we can get from there an excellent class_ of immigrants. We all know the qualities of the Belgians: they are very thrifty, very industrious, and very excellent gardeners. Around our large cities such as Toronto, Montreal, and Winnipeg there would undoubtedly be a large sphere of operations for them. Some are located around Montreal and they are probably the best gardeners on the island. I would ask the minister to enable our agents in Belgium to send, not only in Quebec, but elsewhere our fair share of this very interesting population. The province of Quebec deserves that consideration. The results of every decennial census show that in that province we are doing our duty towards the Dominion, and we are spreading

throughout the whole country. In order to maintain Canada as loyal and as proud as it should be, we should get some recognition from the Minister of the Interior.
In that way, we get from abroad a isprinkling of French blood. It is good blood. Look .at the Anglo-Saxon race, the finest race in the world, after the French-Canadian. It is a mixture of French, Saxon, Dane and many other races. But the Norman predominates in the Anglo-Saxon and is the best part of him. I hope that Mr. Hawkes, who has been employed by the Department of the Interior, to promote co-operation in immigration with the provincial governments, will not lose sight of the fact that, while it is1 a good policy . to have the British-born in Canada, to have the bulk of our immigration from the British Islands-which I approve, sincerely approve-yet we can make excellent British *subjects of those of pure French and Belgian slock. For these people find natural affiliations in this country, not only in Quebec, but in parts of Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan, and in the maritime provinces as well. I was pleased to read the other day the interview given to the papers by Hon. .Richard McBride, the Premier of British Columbia, commending to attention the words of Rudyard Kipling of some years ago, ' pump in the whites,' referring to the need of this policy in order to keep British Columbia as a white mam's country. And Mr. McBride made a special appeal to tire French-Can-adian race, declaring that it was the best race for British Columbia. Send more French-Canadians, was his conclusion, *and British Columbia will be ultimately saved. When I think of six Tories from British Columbia in this House, I cannot but think that the province needs salvation. If we Iliad more French^Canadian inhabitants in Die Rocky mountains, British Columbia would soon give a good account of herself. But, speaking seriously, I hope my hon. friend, who knows the French, having been brought up in the good old county of Argenteuil, will not forget that they have some claims on his department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am sure I have but little fault to find with what my hon. friend has so well said. First, with respect to the matter of co-operation with the province of Quebec, we shall undoubtedly be as well pleased to co-operate in regard to immigration with the province of Quebec as with any other province in Canada. My hon. friend has just stated what 1 already knew, that the province of Quebec has opened offices of its own in London and elsewhere. I believe we gain advantage by working together, especially in respect to literature. The Dominion is preparing literature suit-, able for the different provinces at all times,
and literature suitable for the local governments and under their direction will be distributed by our agent, as well as in the localities in which they may have their agent's offices. So far as immigration from France and Belgium are concerned, and especially with regard to our office in France, I may say that no change has been made in the officers or their salaries. The only change made since I took charge of the department is to provide better and more suitable offices for the officers in that place. My hon. friend correctly states the position which we occupy in sending our agents to France. The government there has adopted a view which the hon. gentleman describes, and we are prevented from pursuing a general policy of immigration such as we pursue elsewhere. We are obliged to do what little work we do under the head of an information bureau. If we con expand, even in that way, I can assure my hon. friend we are ready to increase our staff or do anything more we possibly can to secure additional immigrants from France. We only secured something like
10.000	during the past ten years. And, while as the hon. gentleman says', conditions are a little different in Belgium-we have more freedom there-I think we have only secured
8.000	from that country in twelve years. In the meantime, we . shall be glad, if possible, to introduce assistance there and adopt a more vigorous policy with a view to inducing people in France and in Belgium to take advantage of the many opportunities which offer, not in the province of Quebec only, but in the other provinces as well, for people to better their positions and live under conditions where they can carve out a place for their children and do much better, I am sure, than they could do by remaining at home.

There may be some misapprehension as to the course pursued in the past with regard to co-operation. If it should be thought that there has not been co-operation hitherto, certainly the person so thinking labours under a misapprehension. I know that when I was connected with the provincial government of New Brunswick, the agent-general of that government in London, who had charge of immigration for the province, co-operated with the federal officials and an active propaganda was carried on. It was particularly active between the years 1897 and 1900 inclusive, as I personally know of. And since then the province of New Brunswick has had an agent-general in London whose chief duties were to give attention to immigration matters in eo-operation with the federal Department of Immigration. The late Charles Duff-Miller represented New Brunswick as agent-general for many years. Probably no man has



been, in London more active in immigration to the province of New Brunswick. He saw to it that literature was circulated, and acted with the officials of the Dominion in that regard; and I know that the federal officials were very much disposed to assist him in the work. So we should not run away with the idea that there has been no co-operation in the past between the provincial and the federal governments in this matter. I think it is due to the committee that my hon. friend (Mr. Rogers), should state exactly what new arrangements have been made in this respect, and how far co-operation has been elaborated as between the several provinces and whether they have reached the point where they will probably co-operate more fully than in the past. I presume that that information is in the department. As we understand that an official has recently been appointed to confer with the provincial governments with a view to closer co-operation than in the past, I think it would be an advantage to the country to know what the arrangements are. I suppose there must have been correspondence and other writings with regard to these plans. Several meetings have been held. I would like to know the nature of the understanding, and, if there are any financial features, what they are- whether there is any arrangement for the division of the expenses that are assumed, and have been assumed by the provincial governments in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I appreciate what the hon. gentleman has said with' respect to New Brunswick in particular. I want to endorse everything he has said with respect to the agent-general, Mr. Duff-Miller, whom I had the pleasure of meeting on more than one occasion in London. He certainly was a most worthy representative of the people of New Brunswick, and a credit not only to that province, but to the Dominion of Canada as a'whole. He did much to make pleasant the visit of any Canadian that he met upon the other side while he occupied that position. I can understand that any government will cooperate with and lend assistance to such an individual as was Mr. Duff-Miller, occupying the position which he did in England as the representative of New Brunswick. I had a visit from the Premier and some of the ministers of the province of New Brunswick and we took up this matter. They have a plan of their own in respect to how they propose to divide their work up, and I presume they will announce it in their own legislature in due course. But, I may say to my hon. friend that I gave them the assurance that we were prepared to supply an agent named by the province to represent them at London, England, and to do the work as re-Mr. EMMERSON.
presenting that province, but paid by the Dominion. I also 'told him that we were prepared to give them one or two agents for special work in the province of New Brunswick. This plan is being prepared, and I shall be glad to furnish any information in connection with its progress to my hon. friend.
I would like to ask the minister if he has sent farm delegates to the British Isles this winter?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have followed the general practice and a number have gone. I do not know that we have been able to send as many as went last year, but the number is pretty nearly the same.

So far as I understand the policy of the minister it is to pursue unremittingly the policy of Canadian immigration propagandism that has been pursued by his predecessor. In regard to these farm delegates, my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) will bear me out in what I say, that there were at least two members in what was then the opposition, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) and the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk), who showed tremendous hostility to these farm delegates being employed. I do not call attention to that subject to express any sympathy with their action then, nor to follow the example of their action myself now. But, there are circumstances in the present condition of western Canada that I think should be in the minister's mind in connection with his immigration policy. We had what to me was a very pregnant admission from the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) in this House in another debate the other day. He said that it had to be admitted that for the moment production has outrun transportation in western Canada; that is to say, that production had outrun our present ability to dispose of what we produce. The only object af production is to dispose of what we produce, and, clearly, if we do not dispose of it, it would be better not to be produced. If we are to pursue unremittingly this immigration propagandism the difficulty occurs in my mind that in a few years production must invariably, by the process of logic, still further outrun our transportation and marketing facilities. I do not want to saddle my hon. friend or the government with the responsibility of providing markets, but he is far too clearheaded a man not to see the connection between that part of his departmental work that is now under survey, and the admission of his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Mr. Arthur Hawkes, in the recent election, I understand, made an appeal to the British-born to forego the advantages of a great and freer market.

Mr. Hawkes is now making another appeal to the British-born to come to the same country where he previously pur-suaded their fellow countrymen to forego the advantages of this market.
May I ask the hon. gentleman if he will pardon me-?
No, I will not pardon the hon. gentleman.

I understand he is making a statement in reference to Mr. Hawkes. When did Mr. Hawkes state-
Some lion. MEMBERS. Order, order.
I am going to ask on what occasion did Mr. Hawkes state that he did not want us to have wider markets. Do not put statements in his mouth that he did not make.
One has a great deal of trouble with 'buddin- ministers in this House. I prefer to deal with actual ones. I do not think the Minister of the Interior resents a single word I am saying.
The trouble with the hon. gentleman is that- he was only in the bud as a minister.

I was pointing out a difficulty which I see in connection with the policy of the Minister of the Interior and of the government. I _ think, Mr. Chairman, that I was within the rules of order and pointing the difficulty out and drawing the attention of the government and the minister at present before us to the difficulty in parliamentary terms and in courteous language. My point is that it is due to this side of the House to know what the government means to do in the presence of a difficulty which exists out of the mouth of one of the members of that government. Now, as I have said already, I do not want to saddle the minister or the government with the responsibility of providing the markets, but ;t is very clear that unless this deadlock-because it is that in western Canada to-day-is removed there may be more wisdom than we saw at the time in the contention of the hon. member for Halton and of the present hon. Minister of Public Works that we should hold our hand for a little in this immigration propagandism. I believe that my contention is strictly logical and to the point, and I am sure the minister will bear me no grudge for pointing out this matter to him.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can understand and appreciate the difficulties that have occurred this year by reason of what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clark, Red Deer) is pleased to term the overproduction of grain in 105i
western Canada. It is true, it is a fact, and I am sure that as western members, at all events, we are all proud to notice and declare the fact that we have grown in the three prairie provinces something over 450,000,000 bushels of grain of different sorts. Naturally, ;n view of that great development, we have had very considerable difficulty in securing railway transportation for that amount of produce. However, I see a brighter outlook for the future perhaps than my hon. friend in this regard. We have now under construction two additional transcontinental railways which will be finished in the very near future, I hope, and in addition to these we have the Hudson Bay railway well under way. I am one of those that have confidence enough in the construction of the Hudson Bay railway to believe that we are going to get an outlet there, not jalone for three or four months in the year, butl think that is the only outlet shown on the map of Canada where the people of western Canada will ever be able to get their products transported to the markets, of the world for twelve months in the year. In my judgment, if this government undertake and carry on the _ construction of the Hudson Bay railway to Fort Nelson or Churchill and undertake the construction of a line of railway from the other side of the bay to the Labrador coast, we will be able to have open navigation for twelve months in the year. It is true, as everyone knows, that it would he impossible to secure that by going through the straits, but I think that by avoiding the straits and undertaking the construction of a line of railway such as I have described, we will be able to have, not alone for three or four months in the year but for twelve months in the year, an outlet for the .grain that we produce.
How would you get across Hudson Bay in the winter months?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It does not freeze over during the winter months.
Surely there is ice there.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is ice, but we have ice at Port Arthur and elsewhere. There are ice-breakers that are very convenient for keeping the harbours open in the winter time and I think this is one of the things, at all events, to be considered in the future. Nevertheless, we will get our marlrets and I hope that we will be able to get our transportation in such shape as will lead to greater development and prosperity in western Canada in the future than we have had in the past.

I am rather surprised at the statement made by the hon. gentleman about the Hudson Bay railway. As far as we know navigation through the

straits is possible only for two and a half or three months in the year. I know that Hudson Bay itself is navigable at nearly all times of the year. But my hon. friend says that if we build the Hudson Bay railway from the Pas to Nelson or Churchill and that if we build from the other side of the bay to a port on Labrador we will have solved the question of transportation.
That brings up the question of the construction of what is generally called the James Bay railway. When my hon. friend mentions the Labrador railway, does he mean that this section of the Hudson Bay railway would have its terminus on the Labrador coast? The most popular and feasible route would be one from the head of James Bay following the Nottaway river, tapping the Transcontinental railway at some point and coming in a direct line to Montreal or Quebec. That would solve the question of the transportation from the west at all times of the year. I was speaking to Captain Bernier the other day and he told me there are reports in the Department of Marine which mentioin the fact that Fort Nelson is the most available port taking it all the year around, and that very little work would have to be done at it. In order to solve the Muestion of transportation when the Hudson straits are not open it was pointed out the other day by the Minister of Railways and by Sir Lomer Gouin, Prime Minister of Quebec, that the construction of the James Bay railway from the head of that bay to Montreal or Quebec is the proper course to pursue. It is only five hundred miles long and it traverses a splendid territory, rich in minerals and in lumber, and has fine agricultural land being a continuation of the famous clay belt of Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) but in the development of our country, as he knows, we have to take it step by step. I quite believe that before the suggestion which I threw out a moment ago will be realized we will have in operation the James Bay railway to which the hon. member has referred. In my judgment such an outlet will give a longer period of transportation than would navigation through the Hudson straits.
- I am told there are about nine months navigation that way.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In addition to that, this parliament has already voted a large subsidy for the greater portion of the James Bay railway and I hope it will be carried on and that by the time we get our railway built to Port Nelson or Fort Churchill the James Bay railway will be constructed so that we can make a connection and secure all the advantages that the construction of such a line, would give to the people of western Canada.
Mr. LEMIEUX
What provinces have agents in England now?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not sure but I think British Columbia, Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and 1 think Quebec is starting now.
Nova Scotia has an agent general who is the representative of the province at large.
There is also an agent from Prince Edward Island.
Will these agents be withdrawn -as the result of the scheme of cooperation that is being entered upon?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That will be a matter entirely for the provinces. I think the provinces now feel important -and strong enough to believe that they should be represented by their own agents general who will probably not devote so much of their time to the matter of immigration as formerly, but who will do other work in connection with the provinces which they represent. At least that has been suggested, and I do not know to what extent the practice will be adopted.
In what way will this duplication of work be .avoided, and in what way is the 'expense to be decreased by the co-operation system proposed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Will the minister appoint the men designated by the several provincial governments and will the Federal government pay the salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax)-. Will the Federal government pay the greater portion of the -maintenance and literature?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That has to be arranged
yet.

It is only fair I think that the federal government should bear, if not the whole, the greater portion of the cost, because it is not a fair expenditure to force upon the various provinces.
I think the minister will agree with me that the several provincial governments in this country have all they can do with their limited financial strength to perform the various public services which fall under their jurisdiction, and these are becoming more burdensome on them all the time. I think in the matter of immigration the federal government might well pay all the expenses of the printing of immigration literature for the provinces.
I must say that I fail to see the economy of the arrangement so far as the Dominion is concerned, although, of course, there may be economy in respect of the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not wish to be understood as saying that we will have any increased economy so far as the Dominion is concerned, but we will have increased economy to the extent that between the Dominion and the provinces we will not be duplicating the work, and having two men doing what one man could well do. For instance, the other day the Minister of Agriculture for Ontario arranged with me to join forces in the office in Toronto which is a considerable saving for our department, and he would pay the rental if we would supply him with a certain amount of literature. We save duplicating the work in that way. In a general sense it is not as a policy of economy that we are doing this, but in order that we may work in unity towards the same end.

I quite understand the situation now, and I think it is desirable that the House should understand that the economy is an economy of effort rather than an economy in money. If I njight criticise, I would think that in all human probability the Dominion will have the privilege of bearing a very large share of the cost under the arrangement that is made. It is to be hoped that it will be accompanied by a corresponding increase in efficiency. Does the minister intend to reopen the office at Boston?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, on the 1st of March.
Was the office entirely closed at Boston?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Then why re-open it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We found the necessity of it to a certain extent and _ the closing gave rise to the false impression that we were closing offices in the United States and not going to be as vigorous in our immigration policy towards our neighbours as we had been in the past. We have had a considerable number of applications for information and we found it necessary to re-open the office.
I suppose all the officials employed in that office were dismissed, and I would be very suspicious that the closing of the office was a modus operandi for getting clear of some officials.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member is
mistaken.
What is the explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) will bear me out when I say that the officials who happened to be in charge of that office were not desirable for the carrying out of the work, and in any case whether the office had remained open or otherwise it would have been necessary to dismiss them. They were not suitable for the work. Accidents will happen in all cases and this was simply an accident.
Were Mr. Hetherington and Mr. Copp the only officers- employed there?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, there were one or two stenographers besides.
Whom does the minister intend to appoint?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have not selected any one yet.

I am afraid I can hardly accept the co-operative principle my hon. friend accords me with regard to the Boston office. If I had held the same opinion of the officials there as he holds it would have been my business to have dispensed with them.
While I admit that the officials had their limitations, they had their good parts-. Mr. Hetherington, who was the first agent appointed there, was a New Brunswicker, a man of very good standing in his province, and well known both in New Brunswick and in New England by the New Bruns-

wickers living there, and for that reason it seemed to me that he was a valuable man. I admit that he had attained a considerable age, and was not as active as he might have been, but certainly he had the qualifications for the work. Mr. Copp, who assisted him was a Nova Scotian, and had formerly been a member of this House. He was a younger man than Mr. Hetherington and certainly was an active man, and I would suppose was a suitable agent. I find no fault with my hon. friend. He is responsible to the country for the efficient operation of his department, and has a right to decide on the efficiency of those in the service. But I do not want to leave myself under the imputation of having retained in office persons who were unsuitable. I would be sorry to see the office permanently closed, because I think there is a good field there, on the lines on which we established it, for securing a population for our western country from the maritime province people, who have settled in many thousands in the New England states.
When Mr. Copp and Mr. Hetherington were dismissed, what reason was assigned in the notification to them?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No special reason was given further than that the office was to be closed. It was a recommendation of a departmental officer which brought it about, nothing else.
What salary did Mr. Hetherington get?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: $1,800 a year.
What did Mr. Copp get?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
It was not a very expensive staff. All I have to say is that I do not like the look of the whole transaction. It does not look as if there was departmental candour at least in getting rid of these officials. They were not highly paid officials. In the case of Mr. Copp it has proved to be a great hardship. While not very old, he is well up in years; he is an ex-member of parliament, and has a good knowledge of Nova Scotia, and I think he could have rendered service to the country up to the extent of the small salary he received. It looks as if these gentlemen were dismissed by a policy of fraud and deception. While the reason given was that the office was to be *closed, we are told that the office is to be opened again. Unless the minister will take the ground that they were dismissed for incompetency, I think his action was most unfair. He could not dismiss them for political partisanship. I think the chairman (Mr. Jameson) will bear me out in Mr. OLIVER.
saying that Mr. Copp, since his appointment to that office, has. not taken any part in politics in Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I may say that there was no politics whatever in the closing of this office or in the dismissal of those connected with it. The action was taken entirely on the recommendation of the officials of the department, for the reason that they did not consider either Mr. Hetherington or Mr. Copp capable of fulfilling the duties they were expected to perform. I did not know them myself; I simply acted on the recommendation of officials of the department. There was no outside interference or request of any description with reference to the matter.

In connection with the immigration from the United States, might I remind the hon. minister that some years ago, under his predecessor in office, and under Mr. Sifton, some French-Canadian agents were appointed specially to look after the repatriation of French-Canadians from the New England States? Amongst the agents appointed were some well-known priests who were well acquainted with the various French-Canadian settlements in the New England States, and I must say that they have been quite successful in repatriating several thousand French-Canadians, many of whom have settled in Saskatchewan and elsewhere, I think, in Alberta. As these agents have proved to be very satisfactory in the past, I hope my hon. friend will continue their services. There is a large population of French-Canadians in the New England States. According to the census returns published by the United States government, the population of French origin from Canada in the United States is nearer one million than a half million. This started many years ago-first at the time of the establishment of the cotton factories in the eastern states, and again during the hard times before 1896. And there was quite an influx of French immigration to the United States. Now the tide has turned, thanks to the efforts of the clergy and to the immigration agents who have been appointed in various cities of the neighbouring republic, and quite a number of these people have come back to Canada. I hope the minister will maintain these agents and see that they continue to do their work well. In this way we can recover many of our people who have not foresworn their Canadian citizenship although they are living on the other side of the boundary line.	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) I may say that we are retaining all the officers to wham he has alluded, and that we are favourably considering recommendations for extending this kind of work.

We in the province oi Nova Scotia are particularly interested in the details of the proposed co-operation because we are very desirous of attracting more people to that province for agricultural purposes. I was glad to hear the minister say they hoped to settle in New Brunswick people who would take an interest in market gardening, and presumably agricultural pursuits generally. In Nova Scotia, more particularly the eastern part of the province, we are confronted with a condition of things that is highly detrimental to agriculture. Prior to 1875 and 1876, farming was almost wholly the occupation carried on in that part of Canada. Almost everybody engaged in agriculture and the cost of living was consequently low. Of recent years large industrial centres such as coal mines, and the steel and iron works, have operated and have had the effect of drawing the rural population from the country. The result is that large tracts of land which previously were thickly settled by farmers, are now practically vacant while there are large centres of population entirely unproductive, requiring tremendous quantities of food stuffs. Hence the cost of living in these busy centres of population and industry is becoming alarmingly high. Our only hope and salvation is that we can secure a class of people who will settle on those vacant lands and make them productive. I have talked to the Premier of Nova Scotia upon the subject, and the question is where are we going to locate immigrants if they come or what inducements can they hold out to them. There is abundance of land but it is not owned by the government, and I would therefore suggest to the minister that in order to effect any substantial progress with his policy in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia he should acquire some of this land. It can be got very cheaply and if it were divided into small farms of fifty acres the necessary inducement to immigrants to come and settle on them would be found. Around Sydney and North Sydney there is much good land available out of which splendid farms can be created. The creation of colonies of fifty or sixty farms in my opinion would be highly successful, and in a short time this scheme would practically make its own way. I am very hopeful that the policy announced will be successful. I wish the minister every success and I trust that his plan will promote the settlement of vacant lands in the maritime provinces.

I would sug-best to the minister that in making appointments to the Boston office, it would be desirable to select persons from the maritime provinces who will appreciate the conditions there much better than persons who have lived in the provinces
of Quebec and Ontario. Such a course might also have the effect of influencing immigration from the United States back to the maritime provinces.

As I was in the chair when the question of closing the Boston office was being discussed I wish now to say a word witn regard to that matter. My first intimation that that office was about to be closed, or that any. change had been made in connection with it, was the receipt of a newspaper clipping forwarded to -me from Digby to the effect that Mr. Copp who was in charge of the Boston office had returned home again. Mr. Copp was my opponent in the election of 1908, and he and I have always been on most friendly terms, and I am glad to say the same friendly feeling exists to-day. Immediately upon receiving the newspaper intimation I -vent to the department and made inquiries, and after a time was informed that the change had been brought about as a result of a report by an officer of the department to the effect, I believe, that it was necessary in the interests of the department, and of that branch of the department's work. I also heard at the same time from Digby that Mr. Copp was very unwell. The information given to me at the department was that while the Boston office would be closed on the 31st of December, Mr. Copp had been retired on the 21st of October. I then saw the Minister of the Interior and represented to him that Mr. Copp was unwell, and urged that he be reinstated for the remainder of the period that the office would remain open, that if necessary, Mr. Copp, though too unwell to resume his duties, should be allowed leave of absence and his salary paid as though he were still in the service of the department at the Boston office. The minister acceded to that, and Mr. Copp has been paid his salary up to the 31st of December. Only yesterday I received from Mrs. Copp a letter expressing appreciation of what had been done in that regard, and stating that her husband's health was such thal she regretted his inability to write me himself. I do not want any member of the House to think for one moment that I had ever done or said anything that would militate against the interests of Mr. Copp as an officer of the department, because, as I have already said, we have always been on the best possible terms, and it would be the last thing I should have thought of under the circumstances.
No one has ever suggested such a thing.

I wish to ask whether under this proposed co-operative arrangement as applied to the province of Nova Scotia, that province is to nominate an immigra-

tion agent with a permanent residence in England, at the expense of the Dominion with two or more subordinate agents. All the provinces are represented in the government, excepting Alberta, Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island, and I have no doubt that the ministers representing the other provinces will take care, of the interests of those three provinces in this arrangement. I would ask the minister if the arrangement he has sketched is equally open to Alberta, Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island as to the province of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The same conditions will obtain in all the provinces.

I would like to clearly understand the new policy of the minister as regards this co-operative work between the provinces and the Dominion. If I understand rightly the officers thus working together will be paid the one by the province, and the other by the Dominion. And then the Department of the Interior will see to the literature to be issued to the public. Will the literature tend to move immigration towards the west especially?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, the idea is to have special literature for each province prepared by the representatives there.
The Dominion government will do just as much to help immigration towards the several provinces as towards the public lands of the west.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Just the same.

When we are next in committee on these estimates I should be glad if the minister will give some details about the mission intrusted to Mr. Oliver Asselin. I understand that he has a commission from the department to look after agencies in Europe.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will answer that at once. The mission was simply in connection with the French and Belgian agencies, with a view to widening our scope, the subject we discussed a few moments ago. Mr. Asselin was represented to me as being a suitable man for this Work, and he was going anyway. He receives the same salary as a farm delegate. He undertook the work, and will make a report,
Has the minister received the report?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not yet.

I should be glad if the minister would inform me when it is received. Mr. Asselin is a very able man, Mr. OLIVER.
a splendid writer; I shall be much interested in reading his report.

When we are again in Supply, I desire to ask some questions concerning the application made by some of the East Indian population of British Columbia with regard to the admission of their wives into that province.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman want the information to-night?
No.
As to the agents of the provinces appointed in England, will they occupy a part of the offices provided by the Dominion or will they have separate offices? and if so who will provide these offices?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That has not yet been definitely decided. Some of the provinces are ambitious enough to have their own offices and buildings and wish to remain in them, -while others have not. I think we have reached the time when probably this government should do something about securing large and suitable buildings in London for the purposes of the Immigration Department and other departments of government that are represented over there. If that scheme is carried out in the near future, I hope we shall provide, in that building under whatever arrangement we might make, suitable and acceptable accommodation for each province.

Certainly that is an excellent idea. It is the idea propounded the other day by my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury). One goes to London, and passing along the Strand sees on one side the Ontario building, on the other side the Quebec building; and a little further, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and all using the magic word ' Canada.' Why not have one big central building for the Dominion with all the provinces located in that building? When my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) was Minister of the Interior, a proposition was made by Lord Strathcona to provide for a splendid building in the heart of London. I believe a site could then have been obtained on favourable terms on Trafalgar Square which would have been very suitable. The Department of Immigration has offices on Charing Cross, a small place and occupying a very valuable site, but the display made there, I am sure, has brought thousands of immigrants to this country. Passing there morning, afternoon or evening-for the place is kept bright at night with electric light's, one can always see a crow'd looking at the exhibits in the window. And, as

I say, this is a small corner of Charing Cross, If we had the old hotel in front of the Nelson Statue-I think it is called Morley's hotel, one of the old landmarks-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am told that is a very expensive site.

It may be so; but you cannot have a central site in London suitable for Canada without paying the piper. But look at the Grand Trunk railway, the Canadian Pacific railway, the Allans, and all the big concerns that have erected splendid buildings and that are doing the advertising for Canada. Canada is big enough and rich enough to do advertising for herself. And certainly I would commend the action of the government if they were to erect in the heart of London, which is the heart of the empire, a big building -which would be architecturally beautiful, and would in itself be an advertisement for the country; make it the headquarters of our High Commissioner, and rally all the provinces under that roof.
I think it would be the beginning of a very sane imperialism.
I see that there is an increase of $50,090 in the first item on the list.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
While n appears as an increase it is not such in reality. It is due to the fact that in former years a number of salaries were charged to the vote of contingencies. These were added to the salary list for the year 1912-13. According to a statement prepared early in November, it will require $387,812.26, to pay the salaries of the immigration employees in the outside service, leaving little over $12,000 to provide for new appointments and increases during the ensuing year. While you provided $350,000 you spent $387,817.26 up to November 15. So that it is practically the same thing.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. ROGERS moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Government Bills, and, if we get through with those, Supply.

What Bills?
1 Mr. ROGERS. The Bills on the order paper.
And when we go into Supply we will take up my hon. friend's (Mr. Roger's) estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
